items.title: [COL-09] Build NATS JetStream event ingestion pipeline
items.body:
### Goal
Provide durable transport for normalized discrete events from central and remote collectors.

### Context
See [Master Blueprint](../blob/main/docs/MASTER_BLUEPRINT.md) §7 and [Engineering Rules](../blob/main/docs/ENGINEERING_RULES.md) §6–8.

**Phase:** Phase 3 — Collector and telemetry foundation
**Task ID:** `COL-09`
**Scope**
- Add JetStream development/Compose profile and config.
- Implement authenticated typed publisher/consumer for versioned event envelopes.
- Define subjects, retention, message limit, acknowledgement, retry, replay, and parking behavior.

**Out of scope**
- Do not stream every numeric sample by default.
- NATS is not source of truth.
- No per-device/per-subscriber subjects.

### Specification
- Consumers validate schema/tenant and are idempotent; poison messages are bounded and inspectable.

### Design rules
- Least privilege and network isolation; bounded payload/retry; document stream recovery.

### Dependencies
- [ ] #43 — COL-07
- [ ] #44 — COL-08
- [ ] #11 — FND-11
- [ ] #18 — SEC-05

### Acceptance criteria
[ ] JetStream starts in dev/Compose profile.
[ ] Publisher and consumer exchange valid envelopes.
[ ] Duplicate delivery causes no duplicate side effects.
[ ] Unsupported schema/poison message path is tested.
[ ] Stream/consumer limits are documented.

### Verification
Test publish/consume, duplicate replay, malformed schema, and broker outage recovery.

### AI execution notes
Read product docs and this issue. Inspect existing code first. Implement only this bounded deliverable. Add focused tests. Report changed files, commands, outcomes, and unchecked criteria.

items.title: Placeholder - Database migration service

type.name: Feature
type.description: A request, idea, or new functionality

items.body:
**Future Work:** Design and implement a database migration service for managing schema evolution across data-index deployments.

## Context

As data-index schemas evolve (PostgreSQL tables, Elasticsearch index templates), we need a reliable way to apply migrations in Kubernetes environments. This service will handle:

- Flyway-based PostgreSQL schema migrations (MODE 1 and MODE 3 - both use same normalized schema)
- Elasticsearch index template and ILM policy updates (MODE 2)
- Pre-flight schema validation
- Rollback capabilities

## Proposed Scope (Not Finalized)

**Container Image:**
- Base image with Flyway and Elasticsearch migration tools
- Migration scripts bundled in image (versioned)
- Configuration via environment variables

**Kubernetes Integration:**
- Run as Kubernetes Job (one-shot migration)
- Or as InitContainer for data-index pods (automatic schema setup)
- Health checks and failure handling

**Schema Management:**
- **PostgreSQL (MODE 1 and MODE 3):** Flyway migrations in `data-index/data-index-storage-migrations/src/main/resources/db/migration/`
  - MODE 1: Includes triggers for FluentBit → PostgreSQL normalization
  - MODE 3: Excludes triggers (ingestion service does JDBC UPSERT directly)
  - Both use identical normalized table schema
- **Elasticsearch (MODE 2):** Template/transform JSON in `data-index/data-index-elasticsearch-schema/src/main/resources/schema/`
- Version tracking table (migration history)

**Integration Points:**
- data-index Helm chart references db-migration Job
- logic-operator deploys db-migration before data-index service

## Status

**Blocked:** Needs design discussion and ADR

**Questions to Resolve:**
1. Should migrations run as Job or InitContainer?
2. How to handle multi-tenant deployments (separate schemas per tenant)?
3. Rollback strategy for failed migrations?
4. Schema drift detection and alerting?

## Next Steps

1. Create ADR for db-migration architecture
2. Prototype Flyway Job for PostgreSQL
3. Design Elasticsearch index migration approach
4. Integrate with data-index Helm chart

## Dependencies
None - future work

items.title: Complete FX Replay–grade analytics with broker deal ingestion and per-signal attribution
items.body:
## Goal
Enable users to analyze the **realized outcomes of their own Telegram / TradingView signals**, not just account-wide MT5 P/L, while keeping Cloudflare D1 usage bounded.

## To-do priority and dependencies (2026-11-07)
**P1 — Full FX Replay–style trade analytics and journal for Signal Bridge Client Portal and Telegram Mini App.**
Tracked in the primary implementation backlog; **not complete**. The premium read-only portal shipped in #116, but account-wide daily P/L is not per-signal trade analytics.

**Dependency:** First stabilize/verify D1 after the daily read-limit incident and index/polling patch #111. Do not enable high-frequency queries or retrospective bulk ingestion without bounded batches, indexing and measured row-read budgets.

## Trader-facing deliverables
- [ ] Full **trade history & replay timeline**: signal received → parsed → routed → EA command → broker order/fills → TP1/TP2/TP3/SL/partial exits → closed result; distinguish *delivered* from *broker-confirmed*.
- [ ] FX Replay–style **performance dashboard** with verified Net P/L, gross profit/loss, win rate, profit factor, risk/reward, average R, expectancy, streaks, max drawdown, average trade duration and fee-aware results.
- [ ] **Equity/P&L curve, daily/weekly/monthly performance calendars**, outcome distribution, time-of-day and Asia/London/New York session analysis with timezone/DST handling.
- [ ] **Trade journal** with searchable signal/trade inspector, notes and tags, entry/exit/SL/TP price levels, trade source, strategy and screenshot/chart references only when explicitly available.
- [ ] **Powerful filters**: user/account, DEMO vs LIVE, Signal Bridge vs Scalper Pro (show unavailable when no Scalper telemetry), symbol, date range, session, strategy, Telegram vs TradingView and execution status.
- [ ] Tenant-scoped **CSV export** of broker-verified trade/deal history, with formulas, fee treatment and safe CSV encoding documented.
- [ ] Optional **Monte Carlo / scenario simulations** clearly marked hypothetical, and only with adequate verified history. No synthetic data presented as realized results.
- [ ] Responsive premium UI matching the existing website/Mini App aesthetic; preserve Setup, admin access, licenses and current connection controls.

## Implementation checklist
- [ ] EA `deal-history-v1` capability with idempotent broker deal and position ledger, account binding and replay checkpoint
- [ ] Secure EA→Agent Hub batch ingestion and per-tenant D1 schema for broker deals, trade/signal correlation and partial exits
- [ ] Signal→command→order→position→closed-deal reconciliation, including unassigned/manual trades, netting/hedging and all fees
- [ ] Authenticated tenant-scoped analytics endpoint and daily/hourly incremental aggregates
- [ ] Actual Win Rate, R/R, PF, average win/loss, streaks, trade duration and drawdown (with formula definitions and missing-data states)
- [ ] Hour/day/month performance, annual calendar and Asia/London/New York session grouping with UTC/DST rules
- [ ] Journal, verified trade CSV and deterministic Monte Carlo with sample minimums and clear hypothetical labeling
- [ ] Account-level vs SignalBridge-attributed toggle; filter by EA, symbol, source, time and demo/real account
- [ ] Tests for tenant isolation, duplicate replay, account mismatch, fees, invalid timestamps, limit cases, timezone and D1 query budget

## Definition of done
- [ ] Per-trade analytics reconciles to actual MT5 broker deals and records provenance; incomplete or ambiguous attribution remains explicitly unassigned.
- [ ] Correct handling of SL/TP, partial closes, commissions, swaps, netting/hedging and replay/reconnect without duplication.
- [ ] Real-data-only KPI values, clearly labeled account-wide versus signal-attributed figures and trustworthy missing-data states.
- [ ] Privacy/isolation, mobile/desktop/Mini App, responsive, load, performance and D1 read-budget tests all pass before production release.

Initial read-only UI exploration: #112 (draft). Approved premium client portal: #116 (merged). D1 efficiency patch: #111 (merged). Architecture and acceptance details: `docs/TRADING_ANALYTICS_V2.md` on the #112 branch. Do not use synthetic trading statistics as production data.

## Implementation update — 2026-11-07
- **Draft PR #117** (https://github.com/drfxai/Signal-Bridge/pull/117): first opt-in, read-only broker-deal ingestion from MT5 EA v0.30.0 with account/license validation, D1 idempotent storage, tenant-scoped analytics API, premium trade journal, verified P/L curve, trade calendar, CSV and covered closed-position performance metrics.
- **MetaEditor:** v0.30.0 compiled into a CI artifact with 0 errors; customer release is unchanged.
- **CI:** JS/unit tests passed on the latest branch; browser regression runs and production rollout gates are tracked in #117.
- **Not yet complete:** true FX Replay-style chronological per-signal event replay, reconciled netting and partial positions under all broker behaviors, strategy-R, historical equity, session timezone/DST reporting, user journal annotations, Monte Carlo and scale tests.
- **Deployment blocked:** D1 quota/performance reset verification and staging migration, two separate demo-broker end-to-end tests, and explicit production release authorization. No release or migration has been made.

items.title: Phase 10 Source Explorer + medical library browser + canonical SQLite ingestion
items.body:
## Goal
Build verified **Santo Source Explorer** and **Medical Library Browser** for the user-supplied licensed 7,049 article SQLite corpus: citation -> authenticated original article -> highlight referenced section -> browse nearby sections and all library articles. Desktop panel and mobile full-screen reader. Avoid source leaks or XSS.

## Authority boundaries
- Browser may not supply raw R2 keys, source URLs, tenant or user selectors.
- Citation jumps require existing authenticated verified message/source snapshot and must map exact `libraryId`/`itemKey` to canonical R2 JSON.
- Library browsing remains tenant-authenticated; libraries are currently global and not per-tenant restricted.
- Article display uses strict schema and **plaintext/structured sections**, never raw third-party HTML, script, iframes, data URI or insecure links.
- Only allow media from the approved public R2 media host and normalized `offline_media/` keys. No silent remote image fetch.

## Implementation
- [x] Canonical importer CLI for SQLite -> sanitized article JSON and AI Search-indexable Markdown, versioned stable IDs/section anchors, manifests, checksum and media URL normalization; no licensed bytes committed to GitHub.
- [x] Authenticated source article endpoint with citation snapshot validation and honest section highlight; invalid/stale source must fail closed.
- [x] Authenticated paginated library browse API + article reader without a citation, with bounded query and keys.
- [x] Santo Lit widget reader/side panel, mobile full-screen behavior, section jump and browse UI.
- [x] Royal Bank `/santo` citation control and article viewer integration (or an independent compatible host interface).
- [ ] Full deterministic contract/security tests, staging deploy, authorized browser test, AI Search indexing verification. Do not claim source citation alignment before real indexed corpus.

## Preconditions and acceptance
Owner claims commercial licensing. Do not publish article contents on public R2 or GitHub. Source `all_libraries.zip` is available in ChatGPT container but not on GitHub Actions or Cloudflare R2. Setup private direct ingest with secrets or authenticated uploader. Tests must pass before merge. No full rollout until corpus is uploaded/indexed and validated.

Package `santo_staging_medical_library_r2_bundle.tar.zst` ~29MiB and SHA256 `5123c335926c73489be3957328b652d91d4ee50538cbdddaa62a4ea067a5f9c4`. No corpus bytes added to GitHub.
- Santo post-merge Verify [38500681584](https://github.com/geminiamo0-ship-it/santoreno/actions/runs/38500681584) **SUCCESS**. Staging Worker deploy/401 unauthorized access smoke [38500681521](https://github.com/geminiamo0-ship-it/santoreno/actions/runs/38500681521) **SUCCESS**. **Content upload and AI Search indexing not yet performed** because chat runtime lacks authenticated private Cloudflare R2 object upload. items.title: feat(api): add service-scoped telemetry ingestion credentials
items.body:
## Problem

Headless collectors and agents cannot safely use an end user's OIDC access token. Telemetry ingestion needs a revocable credential that is scoped to exactly one service and cannot be used to read or mutate project data.

## Proposed API

- `GET /v1/projects/{projectId}/services/{serviceId}/telemetry-keys`
- `POST /v1/projects/{projectId}/services/{serviceId}/telemetry-keys`
- `POST /v1/projects/{projectId}/services/{serviceId}/telemetry-keys/{keyId}/rotate`
- `DELETE /v1/projects/{projectId}/services/{serviceId}/telemetry-keys/{keyId}`

Use the existing project-member permission model; do not introduce additional user roles. A telemetry key itself receives only a `telemetry:write` capability.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Generate at least 256 bits of cryptographically secure random key material.
- [ ] Return the plaintext key only once; persist only a digest plus a non-secret prefix for lookup/display.
- [ ] Store key name, service/project IDs, creator, created/expiry/revoked timestamps, and last-used timestamp.
- [ ] Rotation creates a new usable key and safely revokes the previous key with a documented grace-period policy.
- [ ] Unknown and cross-tenant IDs return the same tenant-safe `404` behavior as existing resources.
- [ ] Key create, rotate, and revoke operations produce audit events without logging secret material.
- [ ] Add per-key and per-tenant rate-limit hooks.
- [ ] Document all endpoints and schemas in `postgres-project-tenancy/openapi.yaml`.
- [ ] Add repository, handler, authorization, RLS, and end-to-end tests.

items.title: Fivetran lineage binds same-named tables to the first service in dbServiceNames
items.body:
### Connector

Fivetran

### Feature area

Lineage

### Describe the bug

When several services in `lineageInformation.dbServiceNames` hold a table with the same database, schema and name, the Fivetran connector attaches every connector's lineage to the first listed service.

`_resolve_table` in `pipeline/fivetran/metadata.py` loops over `dbServiceNames` in order and returns the first service where `<service>.<database or *>.<schema>.<table>` exists. It never uses which source the Fivetran connector actually reads from. Sharded or per-tenant estates, where several databases share one schema, are the common case.

In our instance six MySQL services hold the same `evo` schema, one per Fivetran connector. With all six in one agent's `dbServiceNames`, all six connectors' 273 table edges were attached to the first service. Nothing was logged and the run reported success.

### To Reproduce

1. Two database services, A and B, each with table `db.schema.t`.
2. Two Fivetran connectors, one syncing from A and one from B.
3. A Fivetran agent with `dbServiceNames: [A, B]`.
4. Both connectors' lineage originates from A.

### Expected behavior

The source service is chosen from the Fivetran connector's own source (for example its configured host, or its database/service type), or the ambiguity is reported and the edge skipped rather than bound to the first match.

Our workaround is one Fivetran agent per source service, each with a `pipelineFilterPattern` and only its own service in `dbServiceNames`.

### OS

Kubernetes (ingestion-base image)

### Python version

3.12

### OpenMetadata version

2.0.6

### OpenMetadata Ingestion package version

openmetadata-ingestion==2.0.1.0; same logic on main.

### Pre-submission checklist

- [x] I searched for duplicate issues.
- [x] I removed credentials, hostnames, emails, and other sensitive data from logs and config.

milestone.title: Phase 3: SaaS via Template Hub
milestone.description: Exit: broad SaaS coverage through maintained REST/GraphQL templates and Singer targets, without a native crate per API.

items.body:
> **Design spec. Labelled `needs-design`: don't build until every point in "Open decisions" (§15) has a recorded decision.**
> Philosophy (the why, red lines, litmus test) is in the **first comment**; read it before changing anything here.
> Must land first: #1032 (webhook source acknowledges before the sink commits; same ack-after-commit principle the feed cursor relies on).
> Picking this up months later? Start with **"Re-validate first"** at the end.

## Summary
A **feed** is a named, durable, **append-only** log that senders push events into over HTTP. `faucet serve` stores each event in a **pluggable feed store** (SQLite, PostgreSQL, object storage, later brokers and others) and acknowledges only after it is durable. **Consumers** bind a feed to an ordinary pipeline with a **flush policy**. When the policy fires, the feed layer submits a **normal run** whose source (`type: feed`) reads a fixed range of the log, and it advances the consumer's cursor **only after the run's sink commits**.

Feeds are a **layer on top of runs**: they never write to sinks themselves, so transforms, governance, delivery guarantees, DLQ, audit, tenants and metering all come from the existing run path. With no feed configured (or the `feeds` feature off), faucet behaves exactly as today.

```yaml
kind: feed
name: jira-issues
ingest:
  auth: { tokens: managed, signature: { header: X-Hub-Signature-256, secret: "${secret:vault:feeds/jira#hmac}", prefix: "sha256=" } }
  dedupe: { header: X-Atlassian-Webhook-Identifier, window: 24h }
retention: { max_age: 7d, undelivered: { max_age: 30d, max_bytes: 50GiB, on_exceeded: refuse } }
consumers:
  - name: to-iceberg
    pipeline: ./pipelines/jira_to_iceberg.yaml      # source: {type: feed}; sink: iceberg
    flush: { max_events: 5000, max_bytes: 64MiB, max_age: 60s }
```
Senders get `https://<serve>/v1/feeds/jira-issues/events` plus a write-only token or HMAC secret. That's the whole setup.

---

## Design discussion history (chronological)
1. **2026-11-01, discussion #1025:** a user asks for a permanently running webhook endpoint that ingests SaaS events (Jira, GitHub, Stripe, …) into Iceberg without losing events across restarts, comparing it with a streaming database's one-line webhook table. They note that `source-webhook` is a bounded in-memory window and that serve triggers can't pass the body on as records.
2. **2026-11-02, analysis:**
   - The diagnosis is correct. Worse: the webhook source acknowledges `200` before the sink commits, which led to bug #1032.
   - Options compared: a forever-running source (rejected: it fights the bounded-run model), trigger body as data (one run per event harms lake sinks), or an external queue (heavy for simple senders).
   - Proposed instead: a **durable inbox in serve plus micro-batched runs**.
   - Reply posted; the user answered with sizing:
     - SaaS/internal webhooks: 500 to tens of thousands/day;
     - Python analytics apps: up to 100k+/day;
     - a high-volume log bridge: hundreds of GB/day, judged out of scope;
     - file uploads: routed through object storage + `object_arrival`;
     - a single serve instance, about one minute of latency, HMAC for an internal Service Desk.
   - They offered to test a prototype.
3. **2026-11-02, which sources need it:** only `webhook` needs the full design (faucet is the server and senders don't keep data). `nats` (core subjects), `websocket` (live feeds) and `grpc` (non-resumable streams) need the always-on, durable half later, through ingress adapters. Every other source has upstream retention and is safe with bounded runs.
4. **2026-11-02, streaming-vertical exploration:** continuous runs made of checkpointed epochs, with replayable sources first and the durable inbox as the buffer for non-replayable ones. Feeds are the first concrete step; a continuous mode can later replace micro-runs under the same feed layer.
5. **2026-11-03, "channels" idea → named feed:** the owner proposed a first-class concept that keeps taking data, registers it durably, and is picked up by micro-runs. It was compared with a managed delivery-stream service that buffers by size/interval and delivers to sinks. The name **feed** was chosen ("channel" is already used for template channels and notify channels).
6. **2026-11-03, open source:** the whole feature is open source, including multi-tenant, quota, metering and cluster behaviour, consistent with how `faucet serve` already ships tenants, budgets, usage and cluster mode.
7. **2026-11-03, design thought through locally:** pluggable append-only storage, topologies (laptop / single node / Kubernetes / HA / multi-tenant), the safe-watermark invariant, and 22+ edge cases. Then **retention**: 7-day replay retention for delivered events, plus a separate 30-day / 50 GiB hard cap for undelivered events that refuses new events instead of deleting silently. Owner confirmed 7 days.

## Current state (verified on `main`, 2026-11-03)
| Fact | Where |
|---|---|
| `webhook` source: bounded receive window (`timeout_secs` / `max_payloads` / `max_buffered_bytes`), in-memory buffer, HMAC signature verification, constant-time token check; acknowledges `200` on buffering (#1032) | `crates/source/webhook/src/{stream.rs,config.rs}`, README |
| Serve triggers: `webhook`, `object_arrival`, `queue_depth`, `schedule`, with a shared watcher, enqueue + idempotency, health and metrics. `${trigger.body}` is a substitution string only, never records | `cli/src/serve/triggers/` (`watcher.rs`, `enqueue.rs`, `context.rs`, …) |
| Cluster mode: a claim loop pulls `Pending` runs from the shared SQL history DB; member leases and heartbeats; pools (#957) | `cli/src/serve/cluster.rs`, `cli/src/serve/server.rs`, `--pool` |
| RBAC: a closed `Permission` enum (`RunRead`, `RunWrite`, `TriggerFire`, `UsageRead`, `TenantAdmin`, …), with unmapped `/v1` routes falling to admin | `cli/src/serve/rbac.rs` |
| Per-tenant usage metering table `faucet_usage` | `cli/src/serve/history/sql.rs`, `overview.rs` |
| Per-run budgets (`max_records`, `max_bytes`); no ingest-rate quotas | `crates/core/src/budget.rs` |
| Ack-after-commit for message sources (`MessageConsumer::ack` / `ack_pending`), commit tokens (`CommitTokenDriver`) | `crates/core/src/driver/message.rs`, `crates/core/src/driver/sink.rs` |
| Runtime entry point for every serve operation (`Principal` → trust → policy → budget → tenant → governance → execution); a scan test forbids bypassing it | `cli/src/runtime/` |
| Helm chart: Deployment, HPA, PDB, Ingress, PVC, ServiceMonitor | `deploy/helm/faucet-stream/templates/` |

---
Origin: discussion https://github.com/orgs/faucet-hq/discussions/1025 (long-running webhook ingestion), the follow-up with real volumes, and the design conversation of 2026-11-02/03.
Open-source feature of `faucet serve`.

---

## 1. One-paragraph summary
A **feed** is a named, durable, **append-only** log of events that senders push into over HTTP (and later other ingress protocols). `faucet serve` accepts each event, stores it durably in a **pluggable feed store** (DB, object storage, local segment files, an existing broker, …), and only then acknowledges it. **Consumers** bind a feed to an ordinary faucet pipeline with a **flush policy**. When the policy fires, the feed layer **enqueues a normal run** whose source is `type: feed`, reading a fixed range of the log, and advances the consumer's **cursor only after that run's sink commits**. Feeds never move data to sinks themselves: all transformation, governance, delivery guarantees, DLQ and audit come from runs. Turning feeds off, or never configuring one, leaves faucet exactly as it is today.

## 2. Goals
1. **No event loss after acknowledgement:** ack = durably stored in the feed store.
2. **Configuration only:** a sender gets a URL plus a token/secret; no queue or custom receiver to deploy.
3. **A layer, not a fork:** feeds use only existing public machinery (runtime submission, runs, cluster claim loop, leases, StateStore/commit tokens, governance, RBAC, tenants, usage). No change to `Source`/`Sink` traits; existing pipelines are unaffected.
4. **Pluggable storage** behind one append-only log interface; operators choose per feed.
5. **Works on every topology:** laptop, single VM, Kubernetes with many replicas, HA/multi-AZ, multi-tenant.
6. **Micro-batched delivery:** a run per flush (records/bytes/age), never per event (protects lake sinks from small commits).
7. **Fan-out and replay:** several consumers per feed with independent cursors; replay by resetting a cursor within retention.
8. **Observable:** depth, lag, oldest-unconsumed age, ingest rate, rejects, stalled consumers.

## 3. Non-goals (v1)
- Being a message broker: no partitions or consumer-group rebalancing in v1, no cross-region replication, no pub/sub semantics beyond cursors.
- Sub-second end-to-end latency (micro-runs aim at seconds to a minute; the later continuous-run/epoch mode covers lower latency under the same feed layer).
- High-volume log/metrics shipping (hundreds of GB/day, syslog/OTLP firehoses): Vector/Kafka territory.
- Bulk file upload (route through object storage + the `object_arrival` trigger).
- Browser/mobile beacons with public write keys (needs abuse protection; v2).

## 4. Architecture

```
 senders ──HTTP POST──▶ [ingest endpoint]──verify/limit──▶ FeedStore.append ──▶ 202 (after durable)
                          (serve route, any replica)                │
                                                                     ▼
                                                           append-only log per feed
                                                           seq 1,2,3,…  (+ retention)
                                                                     │
  feed trigger (scheduler, one owner per consumer via lease) ── watches head/cursor/age
         │ flush policy met
         ▼
  runtime.submit(run: pipeline + source {type: feed, feed, consumer, range [from, to)})
         │  (normal run: Principal → trust → policy → budget → tenant → governance → execution)
         ▼
  cluster claim loop / local executor runs it → transforms → governed sink write (commit token = feed:consumer:from-to)
         │ run succeeded (sink committed)
         ▼
  FeedStore.commit_cursor(consumer, expected=from, new=to)   ← CAS; only now is the batch "delivered"
```

### Components (all new code is inside the feed layer except one connector)
| Component | Where | Reuses |
|---|---|---|
| `FeedStore` trait + backends | new crate `faucet-feed-store` (+ one crate or feature per backend) | `CallContext`, `faucet_core::http`, fidelity |
| Ingest routes | `cli/src/serve/feeds/ingest.rs` | serve router, body limits, auth middleware, RBAC (new permissions), tenants, audit, metrics |
| Feed registry (definitions, consumers, tokens) | history DB tables `faucet_feed*` (or a `kind: feed` YAML doc loaded like triggers) | history migrations, reload |
| Feed scheduler | **a new trigger kind `feed`** in `cli/src/serve/triggers/` | trigger watcher, enqueue + idempotency, health, metrics |
| `feed` source connector | `crates/source/feed` (a family driver, MessageConsumer-shaped: receive range / ack) | ack-after-commit (#1032 mechanism), commit tokens, `DESCRIPTOR`, conformance |
| Cursor commit on run completion | runtime completion hook | history, leases |
| CLI | `faucet feed create/list/push/tail/stats/cursor/replay/delete` | CLI contract (#1029) |
| Console | Feeds page (depth, lag, consumers, recent rejects) | `serve-ui` (mockups first, per CLAUDE.md) |

### Pluggability / non-interference rules
- Cargo feature `feeds` (in `full`, per the "full means every feature" rule) plus per-backend features. Without the feature: no routes, no tables, no tasks.
- With the feature but no feeds defined: routes return 404, no background work, migrations create empty tables only.
- Feeds call runs **only through `faucet_cli::runtime`** with a `Principal`, like triggers and MCP (the existing scan test forbids calling `run_expanded`/`load_submission*` directly).
- The `feed` source is an ordinary connector: it works in `faucet run` too (see §7), and it declares capabilities via `DESCRIPTOR`.
- Nothing in governance, delivery, state or other connectors changes.

## 5. Data model

### Feed (definition)
```yaml
kind: feed
name: jira-issues
tenant: acme                     # optional; tenant-scoped feeds live under /v1/tenants/{t}/feeds
store: { type: postgres, config: { url: "${secret:...}" } }   # or default store from serve config
ingest:
  auth:
    tokens: managed              # write-only tokens issued via API, stored hashed
    signature:                   # optional HMAC verifier (moved from the webhook source into core)
      header: X-Hub-Signature-256
      secret: "${secret:vault:feeds/jira#hmac}"
      algorithm: sha256
      prefix: "sha256="
      timestamp_header: null
  accept: [application/json, application/x-ndjson, application/x-www-form-urlencoded, text/plain]
  max_event_bytes: 1048576
  max_request_bytes: 10485760
  dedupe: { header: X-Atlassian-Webhook-Identifier, window: 24h }   # or body JSONPath
  rate_limit: { events_per_sec: 200, burst: 1000 }
retention:
  max_age: 7d                 # replay window for DELIVERED events (0 = delete as soon as every consumer has committed)
  max_bytes: null             # optional size cap for delivered data
  undelivered:
    max_age: 30d              # hard cap for events some active consumer hasn't committed
    max_bytes: 50GiB
    on_exceeded: refuse       # refuse (503 + Retry-After, default) | drop_oldest (writes a visible gap marker)
  warn_at: [0.5, 0.8]         # alert thresholds against the undelivered caps
consumers:
  - name: to-iceberg
    pipeline: ./pipelines/jira_to_iceberg.yaml   # or template: owner/name@version + params
    flush: { max_events: 5000, max_bytes: 64MiB, max_age: 60s, min_interval: 10s }
    max_batch: { events: 50000, bytes: 256MiB }  # cap per run (catch-up happens in chunks)
    start: earliest                              # earliest | latest | seq:N | time:RFC3339
    on_failure: { retries: 5, backoff: exponential, then: stall }   # stall | dlq_and_skip
```

### Event envelope (stored per event)
| Field | Notes |
|---|---|
| `seq` | monotonic per feed (per partition later); **assigned by the store**, never by wall clock |
| `id` | ULID (returned to the sender) |
| `received_at` | ingest node clock (informational) |
| `dedupe_key` | from header/body, optional |
| `content_type`, `encoding` | raw body kept; decoding happens in the `feed` source (JSON / NDJSON split / form / text / bytes→base64) |
| `headers` | allow-listed subset only (never `Authorization`, cookies) |
| `payload` | bytes (optionally zstd-compressed in segment backends; optionally sealed with the tenant vault key) |
| `size` | for quotas/metering |

NDJSON / JSON-array requests become **multiple events** in one atomic append (all-or-nothing per request; per-item results are a v2 option).

### Consumer cursor
`(feed, consumer) → committed_seq`, plus `in_flight: {from, to, run_id, lease}`, stored transactionally with the feed store when the backend supports transactions, otherwise in the history DB with CAS.

## 6. Storage backends (all append-only)

### The `FeedStore` interface (sketch)
```rust
trait FeedStore: Send + Sync {
    async fn append(&self, feed: &FeedId, events: Vec<NewEvent>) -> Result<AppendAck>;       // durable before Ok
    async fn read(&self, feed: &FeedId, from: Seq, to_max: Seq, limit: Limits) -> Result<Batch>; // [from, to)
    async fn head(&self, feed: &FeedId) -> Result<Head>;                // safe-to-read high watermark + stats
    async fn commit_cursor(&self, c: &ConsumerId, expected: Seq, new: Seq) -> Result<()>; // CAS
    async fn trim(&self, feed: &FeedId, below: Seq) -> Result<TrimStats>;  // retention
    fn capabilities(&self) -> StoreCaps;  // cluster_safe, transactional_cursor, max_event_bytes, ordering
}
```
The key invariant is the **safe-to-read watermark**: `head()` returns the highest `seq` such that **no event with a lower seq can still appear**. Readers never read past it. This is what prevents the classic "skipped event" bug (see edge case E1).

### Backend catalogue
| Backend | Cluster-safe | Durability on ack | Throughput (rough) | Ordering / watermark technique | Retention cost | Best for |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **SQLite** (WAL) | no (single node) | fsync on commit | low–medium | single writer → seq = rowid; watermark = max committed | `DELETE` + incremental vacuum | laptop, dev, small single node |
| **Local segment files** (append-only log + index, fsync) | no | fsync per group commit | high | single writer per feed | delete whole segments | single node, high volume, no DB |
| **PostgreSQL** | yes | commit (sync replication if HA) | medium | seq from a sequence **+ commit-order watermark** (see E1: snapshot `xmin` / single append-lock per feed / `pg_current_snapshot()`); time-partitioned table | **drop partitions** (cheap) | Kubernetes / clustered serve (history DB already Postgres) |
| **MySQL / MariaDB** | yes | commit | medium | per-feed row lock for seq allocation; watermark = max committed | partitions | shops standardized on MySQL |
| **Object storage** (S3 / GCS / Azure / MinIO): immutable **segment objects** + manifest | yes | segment PUT complete (+ conditional-write manifest update) | high, latency = group window | manifest is the ordering authority; conditional writes (`If-None-Match` / generation preconditions) make manifest commits atomic | lifecycle rules / delete old segments | large volume, cheap long retention, multi-tenant deployments |
| **Hybrid: DB index + object-storage payloads** | yes | both writes done | high | DB holds seq/index/cursor; objects hold bodies (large events spill here) | DB partitions + lifecycle | big events (MB), cheap storage with fast index |
| **Bring-your-own broker**: Kafka/Redpanda, NATS JetStream, Redis Streams, Kinesis, Pub/Sub | yes | broker ack (acks=all / JetStream ack / XADD) | very high | broker offsets = seq; cursor = consumer offset/committed id | broker retention | teams that already run a broker but want the HTTP front door + faucet consumers |
| **Lake table** (Iceberg/Delta as the log) | yes | table commit | medium (commit cost) | snapshot order; must buffer → ack latency = commit interval | expire snapshots | "raw landing zone that is also queryable"; better as a **cold tier** than as the hot log |
| **DynamoDB / key-value** | yes | write ack | high | per-feed bucket + sort key; seq via atomic counter (hot key risk) | TTL | AWS-native serverless setups |

**Tiering (v2):** hot backend (Postgres / local / broker) → compacted **Parquet segments in object storage** after N hours. Consumers read transparently across tiers; long retention gets cheap.

**Recommendation for v1:** SQLite (local), Postgres (cluster), object-storage segments (scale). v2: hybrid, local segment files, BYO broker (Kafka, JetStream, Redis Streams), tiering. Experimental later: lake-table, DynamoDB.

**Capability checks at load:** `serve --cluster` with a non-cluster-safe store (SQLite, local segments) is **refused at startup** with a clear error, so a misconfiguration can't silently split feeds across replicas.

## 7. Topologies

### 7.1 Laptop / local
- `faucet serve` (no cluster) + SQLite or local-segment store under a data dir (not cwd/tmp; 0700 dir, 0600 files).
- **Without a server:** ingest needs a long-lived endpoint, so **ingest requires `faucet serve`**. But the store is a plain backend, so:
  - `faucet feed push <feed> < events.ndjson` appends directly (operator-side tool, uses store credentials, for tests/backfills);
  - `faucet run pipeline.yaml` with `source: {type: feed, feed: x, consumer: y}` drains it once (reads from cursor to the watermark at start, commits cursor after sink). Useful for dev, cron-only setups and replays;
  - a lock/lease on the consumer prevents a CLI drain and a serve-scheduled run from consuming the same range concurrently.

### 7.2 Single node production (VM / systemd / one container)
- serve + Postgres (recommended) or SQLite/local segments on a persistent volume + backups.
- Restart: in-flight runs are re-scheduled from the committed cursor; ingest unavailable during restart (senders retry; document `Retry-After` behaviour and sender retry policies).

### 7.3 Kubernetes, multiple replicas
- **Ingest is stateless:** any replica accepts any feed's events and appends to the shared store (Postgres or object storage). Readiness probe fails while draining so the Service stops routing; preStop finishes in-flight appends.
- **Scheduling:** each consumer has **one owner** at a time, a lease in the history DB (existing lease/member machinery). The owner evaluates flush policy and enqueues runs; on owner loss another replica takes over after lease expiry (no double runs: enqueue is idempotent on `feed:consumer:from-to`).
- **Execution:** runs go through the existing **cluster claim loop** (`Pending` runs in the shared history DB) and **pools** (#957), so feed runs can be routed to a worker pool sized for them.
- **Roles (new, optional):** `faucet serve --role ingest|worker|all` so ingest pods (many, small, HPA on request rate) scale separately from worker pods (fewer, bigger, HPA on queue depth). `all` stays the default.
- **Helm:** values for feed store, ingest Service/Ingress (separate host/path so feeds can be public while the API stays private), NetworkPolicy, PDB, HPA per role, object-storage credentials via IRSA/Workload Identity.

### 7.4 HA / multi-AZ
- Durability = the store's durability: Postgres with synchronous replica (or managed multi-AZ), object storage (regional). Ack only after the store's durable commit.
- Ingest replicas spread across zones; leases survive zone loss (history DB HA).
- **Multi-region:** v1 = independent feeds per region (active/active ingestion, no global ordering); a global feed is out of scope.

### 7.5 Multi-tenant (serve tenants)
- Tenant-scoped feeds: `/v1/tenants/{t}/feeds/{f}/events`; tokens bound to tenant + feed.
- Per-tenant quotas: events/s, bytes/day, storage bytes, number of feeds; enforced at ingest (`429` / `503`).
- Usage metering into `faucet_usage` (events, bytes ingested, bytes stored·hours), the same table the console/overview reads.
- Storage isolation: per-tenant prefix (object storage) / per-tenant schema or row filter (DB); optional per-tenant payload sealing with the tenant vault key.

## 8. Ingest endpoint details
- `POST /v1/feeds/{feed}/events` (+ tenant form). Body: single event, NDJSON, or JSON array (configurable).
- **Auth (feed-scoped, write-only):** feed tokens (hashed, multiple active, rotation, expiry), optional HMAC verifier (generic: header, algorithm, encoding, prefix, timestamp header, tolerance), optional IP allow-list. Feed tokens grant **nothing else**: no read, no run, no admin. **Never** accept serve operator/admin tokens for ingest by default.
- **URL tokens:** some senders can only configure a URL. Allow `?token=` per feed **opt-in only**, redact it in every log/metric/audit line, warn in the console.
- **Limits:** request size, event size, JSON depth, decompression cap for `Content-Encoding: gzip`, rate limit per token/feed/tenant, concurrent connections, slow-request timeouts.
- **Responses:** `202 {ids, first_seq, last_seq}` only after durable append; `400` malformed, `401/403` auth, `409` duplicate (or `202` with `duplicate: true`, configurable since senders differ), `413` too large, `415` content type, `429` rate (with `Retry-After`), `503` store unavailable / feed full (`Retry-After`).
- **Group commit:** concurrent requests to the same feed are batched into one store append within a few ms (throughput) while every request is still acked only after its own events are durable.
- **Dedupe:** by header or body path within a window (store-side unique index or dedupe table), so sender retries don't duplicate.
- **CORS:** off; browser ingestion is v2.

---

## 9. Consumption details
- Flush policy fires when any of `max_events`, `max_bytes`, `max_age` (age of oldest unconsumed event) is reached and `min_interval` has passed; `max_batch` caps one run; backlog drains in consecutive runs.
- The enqueued run carries a **fixed range** `[from, to)` (to ≤ safe watermark). A retry of the same run reads the **same** range, so the sink commit token `feed:consumer:from-to` makes reruns idempotent (exactly-once for sinks with commit tokens; at-least-once otherwise, documented).
- **At most one in-flight run per consumer** (lease + CAS on cursor).
- Run success → `commit_cursor(expected=from, new=to)`. Run failure → cursor unchanged; retry with backoff; after N failures → `stall` (alert, console shows the failing range) or `dlq_and_skip` (move the range's raw events to the DLQ, advance, audit-log it).
- Record-level bad data uses the **existing per-record DLQ**; whole-run failures (sink down, config error) use the retry/stall policy.
- **Replay:** reset a cursor (admin, audited, change-request capable) to `seq`/time within retention, or create a new consumer with `start: time:...`.
- **Config changes:** a run always uses the consumer's current pipeline config; replays re-process with the current config (documented).
- **Ordering:** events reach the sink in `seq` order within a run and runs are sequential per consumer. Event-time order is not guaranteed (senders reorder) → recommend key + updated-at upserts.

## 10. Edge and corner cases (checklist for the spec and tests)
| # | Case | Handling |
|---|---|---|
| E1 | **Skipped events from out-of-order commits** (two appends get seq 10 and 11; 11 commits first; a reader at cursor 9 reads 11, commits cursor 11, then 10 commits → lost forever) | Readers stop at the **safe watermark**: single append lock per feed (simple, limits throughput), or commit-order watermark (Postgres: track in-flight appenders / snapshot `xmin`), or manifest-ordered segments (object storage). Conformance test with forced commit reordering |
| E2 | Run succeeded, crash before cursor commit | Rerun same range; commit token dedupes (exactly-once sinks) or duplicates (at-least-once sinks, documented) |
| E3 | Cursor commit CAS conflict | Means two owners: lease bug or manual reset race → abort, alert, never move backwards silently |
| E4 | Sender retries after a timeout although the append succeeded | Dedupe key; else duplicate is stored (at-least-once ingest) |
| E5 | Store down | Ingest `503 + Retry-After`; scheduler pauses; runs fail fast and retry |
| E6 | Undelivered data reaches its hard cap (a consumer stalled, e.g. sink down over a weekend) | `undelivered.on_exceeded: refuse` (default, no silent loss) → ingest `503 + Retry-After`; `drop_oldest` deletes the oldest undelivered events and **records a gap marker** the consumer sees and reports. Alerts at `warn_at` thresholds before either happens |
| E6a | Retention vs delivery | An event is deletable only when **older than `max_age` AND every active consumer has committed past it**. Deleted consumers never block; paused consumers block (with a warning) and count toward the undelivered cap |
| E6b | Retention clock and granularity | Age is measured from the store's `received_at` (never sender/event time); deletion runs in chunks (partition drop / whole segments / batched deletes), so "7d" means ≥7d and removed within ~1h after |
| E6c | Object-storage lifecycle rules | Not the retention mechanism (they ignore cursors); trimming is explicit. A bucket lifecycle rule is only a backstop set **longer** than `undelivered.max_age` |
| E7 | Consumer added with `start: earliest` after data was trimmed | Starts at the oldest retained seq, records a gap, warns; console/CLI show "replayable from …" |
| E8 | Poison batch (whole run crashes on it) | retries → stall or `dlq_and_skip` per policy; never loop forever silently |
| E9 | Event larger than limits | `413`; or spill to object storage with a pointer (hybrid backend) |
| E10 | Partially invalid batch request | all-or-nothing `400` with item errors (v1) |
| E11 | Clock skew between replicas | ordering never depends on clocks; `received_at` informational |
| E12 | Owner replica dies mid-run | lease expiry → new owner; the claimed run is handled by existing cluster fencing; enqueue idempotency prevents duplicates |
| E13 | Rolling upgrade with a store schema/segment format change | versioned migrations; readers support N and N-1 formats |
| E14 | Feed deleted / tenant deleted | soft delete → stop ingest, finish/cancel consumers, purge after retention; tenant delete purges feeds, tokens, cursors |
| E15 | Token leaked | rotate (multiple active tokens), per-token rate limits, audit of token use |
| E16 | Huge backlog after a long outage | `max_batch` chunks; optional `catch_up_parallelism` (v2, needs partitions) |
| E17 | Non-deterministic transforms on replay (`now()`, UUIDs) | fine with commit tokens; document |
| E18 | Personal data in payloads | retention limits, optional sealing, masking in the pipeline, data-subject deletion = trim by key (v2, hard on append-only stores; document) |
| E19 | Mixed content types in one feed | stored raw with content type; source decodes per event; undecodable → DLQ |
| E20 | Very low traffic | `max_age` guarantees delivery latency; no runs when empty |
| E21 | CLI drain and serve scheduler both active | consumer lease shared by both paths |
| E22 | Backups/restore of the store | restored cursors may be ahead of restored data (or behind) → validate on start, refuse to move cursor past head, report |

## 11. Security (feeds are an internet-facing ingest surface)
- The ingest listener enforces a Host/Origin allow-list and accepts only the configured content types (no cross-site simple requests).
- Separate listener/host for feeds is recommended so the control API can stay private.
- Write-only feed tokens + HMAC, constant-time compare, hashed storage, rotation, expiry, audit.
- Strict limits (size, depth, decompression, rate, connections, timeouts).
- Data at rest: store files 0600 / dirs 0700, DB/object-storage encryption, optional vault sealing.
- Never log payloads by default; redact tokens anywhere they could appear (including URL tokens).
- Threat-model and STRIDE rows for feeds in `docs/architecture/security.md`.

## 12. Observability
Metrics per feed/consumer/tenant: ingest requests by status, events and bytes in, append latency, store errors, depth (head − min cursor), lag (head − cursor), oldest unconsumed age, runs per consumer, run outcome, stalled consumers, retention trims and gaps, dedupe hits. Console Feeds page; alerts (lag > SLA, stalled, near full). Lineage: feed as a dataset (`feed://tenant/name`) upstream of the consumer pipeline.

1. **Phase 0:** #1032, `FeedStore` trait + SQLite + Postgres backends with the watermark conformance suite.
2. **Phase 1:** feed definitions, ingest route (tokens, HMAC, limits, dedupe, group commit), `feed` source, `feed` trigger (flush policy, leases, ranges, cursor CAS), CLI `faucet feed`, metrics, docs, Helm values. Single node + cluster on Postgres.
3. **Phase 2:** object-storage segment backend, hybrid large-event spill, `--role ingest|worker`, console page (mockups first), tenant quotas + usage metering, replay tooling.
4. **Phase 3:** BYO broker backends (Kafka, JetStream, Redis Streams), local segment files, tiering to Parquet, per-feed partitions + parallel consumers.

## 15. Open decisions
1. Feed definitions: YAML docs loaded like triggers, API/DB-managed objects, or both (recommend both: YAML for GitOps, API for the console and automation).
2. Watermark technique per backend (single append lock first, commit-order watermark later?).
3. Duplicate response: `409` vs `202 duplicate:true`.
4. ~~Retention defaults~~ **Decided 2026-11-03: 7 days** replay retention for delivered events (covers a weekend outage plus time to notice; matches common broker defaults; cheap at expected volumes) and a **30-day / 50 GiB** hard cap for undelivered events with `on_exceeded: refuse`. Alternatives considered: 1 day (Firehose/Kinesis-like, less personal data at rest, but no replay window after a weekend outage). Server-wide default + per-feed override + optional per-tenant maximum (per-tenant retention tiers).
5. Default store when none is configured: the history DB backend (SQLite/Postgres) vs a dedicated data dir.
6. Roles (`--role`) in phase 1 or 2.
7. Payload sealing default for tenant feeds.
8. Partitions: per-feed key partitioning in v1 or later.
9. Whether the `feed` source is usable from `faucet run` without serve (recommended yes, with the shared lease).
10. Delete-by-key (data-subject deletion) on append-only backends: later phase; short retention is the v1 mitigation.

## Alternatives considered
| Alternative | Pros | Cons | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Forever-running webhook source** (never-ending run that flushes and keeps listening) | Small change to an existing connector | Fights the bounded-run model (state, exactly-once, governance per run); in-memory buffering; one process owns the endpoint (no HA) | Rejected |
| **Trigger body as data** (one run per webhook) | Very small change | One run and one sink commit per event: lake sinks get small-file/metadata explosion; heavy per-run overhead | Rejected (micro-batching required) |
| **"Use an external queue"** (Kafka/Redis/SQS in front, existing sources behind) | Works today, scales | Defeats "paste a URL" simplicity; extra infrastructure for low-volume senders | Kept as the documented high-volume path; feeds can later front an existing broker as a store backend |
| **Feeds writing directly to sinks** (no runs underneath) | Lower latency | A second delivery path that skips governance, DLQ, exactly-once, audit | Rejected (red line) |
| **One storage backend only** (e.g. Postgres) | Simpler | Locks out laptop use (SQLite), cheap long retention (object storage) and existing brokers | Rejected; pluggable `FeedStore` |
| **Continuous runs (epochs) instead of micro-runs** | Seconds-level latency | Larger engine change; not needed for minute-level use cases | Deferred; can replace micro-runs under the same feed layer |

## Risks
| Risk | Mitigation |
|---|---|
| Skipped events from out-of-order commits (E1) | Safe-watermark invariant per backend + a conformance test that forces commit reordering |
| A stalled consumer silently loses data | Undelivered data is never deleted by age; hard cap refuses ingest (or drops with a visible gap marker); alerts at 50/80% |
| An internet-facing ingest surface | Write-only feed tokens, HMAC, Host/Origin allow-list, strict content types and limits, separate listener/host, data-at-rest protections (§11) |
| Scope creep into a broker or log shipper | Non-goals (§3); a high-volume path stays "use a broker" (optionally as a feed store backend) |
| Per-run overhead at small flush intervals | `min_interval`; continuous mode later for low latency |
| Storage growth / cost | Retention, quotas, `faucet_usage` metering of stored bytes |

## Assumptions
- Runs remain the only path that writes to sinks; `faucet_cli::runtime` stays the single entry point.
- The history DB (SQLite/Postgres) remains available as the place for feed metadata, leases and cursors.
- Event sizes are KB to low MB; larger payloads go to object storage (hybrid backend).
- Senders retry on non-2xx / timeouts at least a few times.

items.title: Schema lifecycle governance: versioned packs, lock vs flexible fields, migration/backfill, promotion gates
items.body:
## Summary

Schema governance is partial. Field constraints exist in reject/warn modes, but there is no full runtime governance model for customer-production data domains: no versioned schema lifecycle with migration/backfill, and key fields can't yet be locked with a managed promotion path.

## Motivation

Customer deployments need locked, governed schemas for their core data domains — not rapid ad-hoc evolution. A domain "schema pack" should have identity fields + core relationships locked, while descriptive/custom fields stay flexible (warn-mode) so external custom fields don't break ingestion.

## Scope

- Versioned schema lifecycle: additive-by-default; explicit migration/backfill process for breaking changes
- Promote key fields from warn to reject mode with documentation
- Environment promotion (dev → staging → prod) with sign-off
- Approval gates for schema changes, new required fields, new tenants
- A packaging concept for a domain schema+relationship set ("locked vs flexible")

## Acceptance criteria

- A schema pack can lock identity fields + core edges while leaving other fields warn-mode
- A breaking change requires an explicit, auditable migration step
- Schema changes flow through an approval gate rather than activating silently

## Related

Ties into per-tenant governance and the constraints/schema-mode work already in the codebase.

---
owner: platform
depends_on: []
blocks: []
spec_sections: ["§9.1"]
blueprint_sections: ["§XVII HUSLFi"]
maturity_target: organized
acceptance:
  - Plaid Link SDK integrated in Client Workspace: /vault/connect-bank route, Plaid Link initialization, public token exchange, access token stored encrypted in vault schema
  - Plaid access token management: per-tenant per-institution Plaid Item stored in plaid_items table (tenant_id, item_id, access_token_encrypted, institution_id, status, created_at)
  - Transaction ingestion: historical 24 months pulled on first connection; nightly incremental sync via Plaid transactions/get; stored in financial_transactions table
  - Cash flow signal extraction: monthly_revenue, monthly_expenses, avg_monthly_balance, revenue_volatility, and overdraft_count computed from transaction history; written to cash_flow_signals table
  - Plaid webhook handler at POST /webhooks/plaid: handles TRANSACTIONS_REMOVED, INITIAL_UPDATE, HISTORICAL_UPDATE, ERROR events; idempotent processing; emits plaid.transactions.updated event on EventBridge
  - Balance monitoring: daily balance check via Plaid accounts/get; writes to account_balances table; low-balance alert when any account drops below 30-day minimum
  - Consent and disclosure: Plaid connection consent captured in compliance.audit_log per FCRA; user can disconnect any Plaid item via /vault/disconnect-bank/:itemId
  - Error handling: Plaid ITEM_LOGIN_REQUIRED triggers reconnect flow in Client Workspace; Plaid rate limits respected via exponential backoff

## Details

Spec §9.1 defines the Plaid Financial Data integration. No existing issue covers §9.1. The integration is referenced in §9.7 (HUSLFi/HUSLConnect bridge) but only as a bridge endpoint, not as the core Plaid integration itself: the Link flow, access token management, transaction ingestion, cash flow signal computation, and webhook handler.

Plaid is the financial intelligence backbone of the platform. Without it, cash flow signals are missing from the diagnostic, the HUSLFi Projection Builder has no data, and the 4-Stage Pipeline Stage 2 cannot wire HUSLFi to the platform.

items.title: feat: Scalability — SaaS multi-tenant architecture with Azure as first cloud
items.body:
## Goal

Make PatchHound production-ready for SaaS multi-tenant deployments. Target scale: many tenants, each with up to ~10k devices and ~50k vulnerability records, with the architecture remaining correct and safe under horizontal scaling.

Azure is the first supported cloud. The self-hosted path (docker-compose / on-premises container runtime) remains a first-class supported deployment option alongside Azure, sharing as much application-level code as possible.

---

## Current state

| Area | Current behaviour | Problem |
|---|---|---|
| Ingestion pipeline | `GetAllPagesAsync` accumulates all pages in a single in-memory `List<T>` before processing (up to `MaxPages = 1000`) | Memory spike per large tenant; not safe at scale |
| Worker concurrency safety | Only `EnrichmentWorker` has a DB-level compare-and-swap lease. `IngestionWorker`, `SlaCheckWorker`, `WorkflowWorker`, `ApprovalExpiryWorker`, `ScanSchedulerWorker`, `RemediationAiWorker` have **no** distributed lease | Running two worker instances causes double-processing (duplicate ingestion runs, duplicate SLA notifications, double approval expiry) |
| Ingestion dispatch | Ingestion runs are triggered by a 1-minute poll loop in `IngestionWorker` evaluating every `TenantSourceConfiguration` cron schedule | All tenant ingestion jobs contend on the same single worker; no backpressure; no dead-letter; no retry on partial failure |
| Redis | `StackExchange.Redis` is referenced and registered but has **zero injection sites** — it is wired up but never used | Prepared infrastructure with no active functionality |
| SignalR backplane | `AddSignalR()` with no backplane. Multi-instance API deployments would silently drop notifications for users connected to a different instance | API cannot be safely scaled horizontally |
| Rate limiting | `PartitionedRateLimiter` with `FixedWindowRateLimiter` — in-process only | Rate limit is per-instance, not per-user across the cluster |
| DB migration race | `MigrateAsync` runs at startup in every API replica with a retry loop | Concurrent replicas race on migration; no distributed lock guards this |
| Observability | Zero Application Insights, OpenTelemetry, or structured telemetry packages. Built-in `ILogger<T>` only | No distributed tracing, no metrics, no alerting surface |
| IaC | `infra/` directory exists with the correct structure (`modules/control-plane`, `modules/shared`, `modules/stamp`, `stacks/azure`, `stacks/selfhosted`, `params/dev`, `params/prod`) but **all directories are empty** | No deployable infrastructure definition |

---

## Scope

This issue covers three work streams that should be implemented together or in close sequence:

---

### 1. Ingestion pipeline — Azure Service Bus + streaming

Replace the in-process poll-and-accumulate ingestion model with a queue-backed streaming model.

**Queue dispatch:**
- `IngestionWorker` cron evaluation remains but instead of running ingestion inline, it **enqueues a message** to Azure Service Bus for each due `TenantSourceConfiguration`
- Message payload: `{ TenantId, SourceConfigId, TriggeredAt, ManualRequest: bool }`
- Separate worker (or competing consumers on the same worker) dequeues messages and calls `IngestionService.RunIngestionAsync` per message
- Dead-letter queue for failed ingestion runs; retry count configurable per tenant
- Self-hosted path: use an in-process `System.Threading.Channels.Channel<T>` as the queue abstraction with the same interface, so the application code is identical and only the DI registration differs

**Streaming ingestion:**
- Replace `GetAllPagesAsync` (`src/PatchHound.Infrastructure/VulnerabilitySources/DefenderApiClient.cs:260`) with `IAsyncEnumerable<TItem>` streaming — yield each page's items as they arrive
- `IVulnerabilityBatchSource` / `IAssetInventoryBatchSource` already exist as cursor-based batch interfaces; the full-accumulation mode in `FetchAssetBatchAsync` (`DefenderVulnerabilitySource.cs:252`) should be replaced with the batch interface
- Ingestion checkpoints (`IngestionCheckpoint` entity) should be persisted after each page/batch so a failed run can resume rather than restart from the beginning

**Interface:**
```csharp
// Abstract over Service Bus vs in-process channel
public interface IIngestionJobQueue
{
    Task EnqueueAsync(IngestionJobMessage message, CancellationToken ct);
    IAsyncEnumerable<IngestionJobMessage> DequeueAsync(CancellationToken ct);
}
```

**Affected files:**
- `src/PatchHound.Infrastructure/VulnerabilitySources/DefenderApiClient.cs` — `GetAllPagesAsync` (line 260)
- `src/PatchHound.Infrastructure/VulnerabilitySources/DefenderVulnerabilitySource.cs` — `FetchAssetBatchAsync` (line 252)
- `src/PatchHound.Worker/IngestionWorker.cs` — replace inline execution with enqueue
- `src/PatchHound.Infrastructure/Services/IngestionService.cs` — Phase 3 rewrite target (already a no-op stub)
- New: `src/PatchHound.Infrastructure/Queues/IIngestionJobQueue.cs`
- New: `src/PatchHound.Infrastructure/Queues/ServiceBusIngestionJobQueue.cs` (Azure)
- New: `src/PatchHound.Infrastructure/Queues/InProcessIngestionJobQueue.cs` (self-hosted)

---

### 2. Worker concurrency safety — DB lease extension

Extend the DB-level compare-and-swap lease pattern from `EnrichmentWorker` to all workers that currently have no concurrency guard.

The `EnrichmentWorker` pattern (`src/PatchHound.Worker/EnrichmentWorker.cs:415`):
- Conditional `ExecuteUpdateAsync` where `LeaseId IS NULL OR LeaseExpiresAt < NOW()`
- Lease owner: `$"{Environment.MachineName}:{Environment.ProcessId}"`
- Lease duration: configurable per worker type
- Released in a `finally` block

**Workers requiring lease protection:**

| Worker | Poll interval | Idempotency risk | Lease duration |
|---|---|---|---|
| `IngestionWorker` | 1 min | Duplicate ingestion run per source | 10 min |
| `SlaCheckWorker` | 1 hr | Duplicate SLA notifications | 2 hr |
| `WorkflowWorker` | 1 min | Double-processing of workflow timeout transitions | 5 min |
| `ApprovalExpiryWorker` | 15 min | Double auto-denial of expired approvals | 30 min |
| `ScanSchedulerWorker` | 60 s | Duplicate scan scheduling | 5 min |
| `RemediationAiWorker` | 10 s | `RemediationAiJob` picked by two workers simultaneously (no optimistic concurrency guard) | 2 min |

**`RemediationAiWorker` additional fix:** Add EF Core optimistic concurrency (`[Timestamp]` / `rowversion`) or a status CAS (`UPDATE ... WHERE Status = 'Pending' RETURNING id`) on `RemediationAiJob` so the job cannot be claimed by two workers atomically.

**DB schema change:** Add `LeaseId`, `LeaseOwner`, `LeaseExpiresAt` columns to a new `WorkerLease` table (keyed by worker type name), rather than adding lease columns to every domain table. Alternatively add a `WorkerLeaseService` that wraps the pattern.

**Affected files:**
- `src/PatchHound.Worker/IngestionWorker.cs`
- `src/PatchHound.Worker/SlaCheckWorker.cs`
- `src/PatchHound.Worker/WorkflowWorker.cs`
- `src/PatchHound.Worker/ApprovalExpiryWorker.cs`
- `src/PatchHound.Worker/ScanSchedulerWorker.cs`
- `src/PatchHound.Worker/RemediationAiWorker.cs`
- New: `src/PatchHound.Infrastructure/Services/WorkerLeaseService.cs`
- New migration: `AddWorkerLeaseTable`

---

### 3. Horizontal API scaling fixes

#### SignalR backplane
- Azure path: replace `AddSignalR()` with `AddSignalR().AddAzureSignalR(connectionString)` or `.AddStackExchangeRedis(redisConnectionString)` in `src/PatchHound.Api/Program.cs` (line 427)
- Self-hosted path: use `AddStackExchangeRedis` with the existing Redis connection string
- Redis is already registered in DI (`DependencyInjection.cs:28`); promote it to a required dependency for both paths once the backplane is wired up

#### Distributed rate limiting
- Replace `System.Threading.RateLimiting.FixedWindowRateLimiter` (in-process) with a Redis-backed implementation (e.g. using `StackExchange.Redis` with a sliding window Lua script, or the `RedisRateLimiting` library)
- Self-hosted path: same Redis instance used for the backplane

#### DB migration race on startup
- Guard `MigrateAsync` with a distributed lock before applying migrations
- Azure path: use an Azure Storage blob lease or a simple `SELECT pg_try_advisory_lock(constant)` PostgreSQL advisory lock (no extra dependency) to ensure only one replica migrates at a time
- Both paths can use the PostgreSQL advisory lock approach since Postgres is shared

**Affected files:**
- `src/PatchHound.Api/Program.cs` — lines 427, 431–450, 470–480
- `src/PatchHound.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.cs` — line 27

---

### 4. Observability

Add structured telemetry as a first-class concern — required before any production cloud deployment.

- **OpenTelemetry SDK** (`OpenTelemetry.Extensions.Hosting`, `OpenTelemetry.Instrumentation.AspNetCore`, `OpenTelemetry.Instrumentation.EntityFrameworkCore`, `OpenTelemetry.Instrumentation.Http`)
- **Azure path:** Export to Azure Monitor (`Azure.Monitor.OpenTelemetry.AspNetCore`) — single package wires up traces, metrics, and logs to Application Insights
- **Self-hosted path:** Export to OTLP endpoint (Jaeger / Grafana / etc.) via `OpenTelemetry.Exporter.OpenTelemetryProtocol`
- Key traces to add: ingestion run per source, per-tenant vulnerability reconciliation, workflow stage transitions, enrichment job execution
- Metrics: ingestion job queue depth, jobs processed/failed per minute, p99 DB query latency, active workflow count per tenant
- Configuration key: `Telemetry:Endpoint` (OTLP) or `ApplicationInsights:ConnectionString` (Azure)

**Affected files:**
- All `.csproj` files — add OpenTelemetry packages
- `src/PatchHound.Api/Program.cs` — `AddOpenTelemetry()` registration
- `src/PatchHound.Worker/Program.cs` — same
- New: `src/PatchHound.Infrastructure/Telemetry/PatchHoundActivitySource.cs`

---

### 5. Azure IaC — Bicep

Fill the `infra/` directory with a deployable Bicep structure. The existing directory layout maps naturally to Bicep modules:

```
infra/
  modules/
    control-plane/    # Azure Container Registry, Key Vault (if not using OpenBao), Log Analytics workspace
    shared/           # PostgreSQL Flexible Server, Azure Cache for Redis, Azure Service Bus namespace
    stamp/            # Container Apps environment, API container app, Worker container app, Managed Identity
  stacks/
    azure/            # main.bicep — composes control-plane + shared + stamp
    selfhosted/       # docker-compose.yml already exists; document it here
  params/
    dev/              # dev.bicepparam
    prod/             # prod.bicepparam
```

**Target Azure services:**

| Component | Azure service | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| API | Azure Container Apps | Auto-scaling on HTTP concurrency; HTTPS ingress; min replicas = 1 |
| Worker | Azure Container Apps (internal) | Scale on Service Bus queue depth (KEDA rule); min replicas = 1 |
| Database | Azure Database for PostgreSQL Flexible Server | General-purpose tier, zone-redundant HA for prod |
| Cache / backplane | Azure Cache for Redis | Basic SKU for dev, Standard for prod |
| Ingestion queue | Azure Service Bus | Standard tier; one namespace, one queue per deployment |
| Secrets | Azure Key Vault (production) or OpenBao (self-hosted / dev) | MSAL managed identity auth for Key Vault |
| Container registry | Azure Container Registry | Geo-replicated for multi-region prod |
| Observability | Azure Monitor + Application Insights workspace | Connected to Log Analytics workspace |
| Identity | User-assigned Managed Identity | Assigned to both Container Apps; used for ACR pull, Key Vault, Service Bus access |

**Authentication between PatchHound and Azure services:**
- API and Worker use a **user-assigned managed identity** — no connection string secrets for Azure-managed services
- `Azure.Identity.DefaultAzureCredential` already referenced (`Azure.Identity 1.18.0` in `PatchHound.Infrastructure.csproj:12`) — use `ManagedIdentityCredential` in prod, `DefaultAzureCredential` in dev

**Self-hosted stack:**
- `infra/stacks/selfhosted/` documents the docker-compose deployment (existing `docker-compose.yml`)
- Service Bus replaced by in-process Channel via `InProcessIngestionJobQueue`
- Redis is already in docker-compose
- OpenBao remains as the secrets backend

---

## Acceptance criteria

### Ingestion
- [ ] Ingestion jobs are enqueued to Azure Service Bus (Azure path) or in-process Channel (self-hosted path) when their cron schedule is due
- [ ] A failed ingestion job is dead-lettered after N retries and does not block subsequent jobs for the same or other tenants
- [ ] `GetAllPagesAsync` is replaced with `IAsyncEnumerable<T>` streaming — at no point is the full page list held in memory
- [ ] Ingestion checkpoints survive a worker restart; the next run resumes from the last saved cursor position
- [ ] A tenant with 10k devices and 50k vulnerabilities can be ingested end-to-end without OOM

### Worker safety
- [ ] Running two worker instances simultaneously does not produce duplicate ingestion runs, duplicate SLA notifications, or double-processed workflow transitions
- [ ] `RemediationAiJob` cannot be claimed by two workers in the same atomic operation
- [ ] Lease expiry and release are visible in logs

### API horizontal scaling
- [ ] Two API instances behind a load balancer deliver SignalR notifications correctly regardless of which instance a user is connected to
- [ ] Rate limiting is enforced per user across the cluster (not per-instance)
- [ ] DB migrations are applied by exactly one replica on startup

### Observability
- [ ] Distributed traces are emitted for all ingestion runs, enrichment jobs, and workflow transitions
- [ ] A `/metrics` endpoint (or Azure Monitor workspace) shows ingestion queue depth, jobs/min, p99 DB latency
- [ ] Application Insights (Azure) or OTLP exporter (self-hosted) is wired up and receiving data

### IaC
- [ ] `bicep build infra/stacks/azure/main.bicep` succeeds with no errors
- [ ] `az deployment sub create` with dev params deploys a working environment to Azure
- [ ] Managed identity is used for all Azure service access (no secrets in environment variables for Azure-managed services)
- [ ] `docker-compose up` (self-hosted) continues to work end-to-end after all application changes

---

## Out of scope

- Read replicas / DB horizontal scaling — not required at the SaaS multi-tenant target scale; re-evaluate if p99 query latency exceeds SLA at >50 active tenants
- Multi-region / geo-distribution — not in scope for the first Azure stack
- DB sharding / per-tenant schemas — current single-schema multi-tenant design is sufficient at target scale with proper indexing

---

## Dependencies

- Phase 3 of #17 (canonical ingestion pipeline rewrite) must land before the ingestion queue and streaming work is built — `IngestionService.RunIngestionAsync` is currently a no-op stub
- Issue #20 (Defender for Cloud DevOps ingestion) should be implemented on top of the streaming interface introduced here

---

## Reference files

- `src/PatchHound.Worker/IngestionWorker.cs` — current cron-poll dispatcher
- `src/PatchHound.Infrastructure/VulnerabilitySources/DefenderApiClient.cs` — `GetAllPagesAsync` (line 260)
- `src/PatchHound.Infrastructure/VulnerabilitySources/DefenderVulnerabilitySource.cs` — `FetchAssetBatchAsync` (line 252)
- `src/PatchHound.Worker/EnrichmentWorker.cs` — reference lease pattern (line 415)
- `src/PatchHound.Api/Program.cs` — SignalR (line 427), rate limiter (line 431), migration (line 470)
- `src/PatchHound.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.cs` — Redis registration (line 28)
- `infra/` — empty directory tree to be filled
