```python
    result['after'] = {'forward': read('forward'), 'backward': read('backward'), 'count_over_time': count(SELECTOR),
                       'matching': count(DELETE_QUERY)}
    result['expected_after'] = {'forward': KEPT, 'backward': KEPT, 'count_over_time': 6, 'matching': 0,
                                'compactor_deleted_lines': 6}
    print(json.dumps(result))
finally:
    stop()
    log.close()
    print(f'loki log and data: {work}', file=sys.stderr)
```

</details>

### Expected behavior

After the purge, the 6 odd lines (`index` 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11) are kept and the 6 even lines are gone, for every read:

```json
"expected_after": {"forward": [1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11], "backward": [1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11], "count_over_time": 6, "matching": 0, "compactor_deleted_lines": 6}
```

### Actual behavior

Before the delete, every read is complete in all four runs: forward and backward return all 12 lines, `count_over_time` is 12 and the matching count is 6.

After the delete (`matching` is the `count_over_time` of the delete query, `compactor_deleted_lines` is `loki_compactor_deleted_lines`):

| Loki | scenario | forward | backward | count_over_time | matching | compactor_deleted_lines |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 3.7.7 | normal | `[]` | `[1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11]` | 3 | 0 | 6 |
| 3.7.7 | crossing | `[]` | `[1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11]` | 3 | 0 | **9** |
| 3.7.9 | normal | `[]` | `[1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11]` | 3 | 0 | 6 |
| 3.7.9 | crossing | `[]` | `[1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11]` | 3 | 0 | **9** |

Querier log after the purge (3.7.9, crossing; the data folder shown as `<dir>`):

```
level=error caller=parallel_chunk_fetch.go:74 msg="error fetching chunks" err="failed to load chunk 'fake/db11d501f9d5fa34/MWExOTQ1ZWMwNDA6MWExOTQ3MTBmYzA6Yzg5M2NiNjA=': open <dir>/chunks/fake/db11d501f9d5fa34/MWExOTQ1ZWMwNDA6MWExOTQ3MTBmYzA6Yzg5M2NiNjA=: no such file or directory"
caller=spanlogger.go:152 user=fake level=error msg="failed downloading chunks" err="failed to load chunk 'fake/db11d501f9d5fa34/MWExOWEzMzBmODA6MWExOWEzN2EzNjA6MTc0OWIxOGQ=': open <dir>/chunks/fake/db11d501f9d5fa34/MWExOWEzMzBmODA6MWExOWEzN2EzNjA6MTc0OWIxOGQ=: no such file or directory"
```

Compactor log for the same run: the request is split into 4 sub-requests of 24h, whose counts add up to 9:

```
caller=request_handler.go:99 msg="delete request for user added" delete_request_id=38e237c9 user=fake query="{job=\"lab\"} |~ \"secret=[A-Za-z0-9]\"" interval=24h0m0s
caller=delete_requests_manager.go:541 msg="delete request for user marked as processed" delete_request_id=38e237c9 sequence_num=0 user=fake deleted_lines=4
caller=delete_requests_manager.go:541 msg="delete request for user marked as processed" delete_request_id=38e237c9 sequence_num=1 user=fake deleted_lines=2
caller=delete_requests_manager.go:541 msg="delete request for user marked as processed" delete_request_id=38e237c9 sequence_num=2 user=fake deleted_lines=3
caller=delete_requests_manager.go:541 msg="delete request for user marked as processed" delete_request_id=38e237c9 sequence_num=3 user=fake deleted_lines=0
```

Chunk objects in `<dir>/chunks/fake/db11d501f9d5fa34/` after the purge (key base64-decoded to `from:through:checksum`, times in UTC):

| object (decoded) | from | through | state |
|---|---|---|---|
| `1a1945ec040:1a194710fc0:c893cb60` | 10-31 23:50 | 11-01 00:10 | original chunk 1: removed, still read by the querier |
| `1a19a330f80:1a19a37a360:1749b18d` | 11-02 03:00 | 11-02 03:05 | original chunk 2: removed, still read by the querier |
| `1a1945ec040:1a19a37a360:dd78702e` | 10-31 23:50 | 11-02 03:05 | rewritten; its range spans both original chunks |
| `1a1946269c0:1a194710fc0:d0cbc17c` | 10-31 23:54 | 11-01 00:10 | rewritten |
| `1a19a33f9e0:1a19a37a360:b5bc580d` | 11-02 03:01 | 11-02 03:05 | rewritten |

The normal run shows the same shape: the rewritten `1a19543a200:1a19a37a360` (11-01 04:00 through 11-02 03:05) spans both original chunks, and the originals `1a19543a200:1a1954835e0:9116ff45` and `1a19a330f80:1a19a37a360:1749b18d` are removed but still requested by the querier.

So it looks as if the index still points at the removed original chunks (reads that reach them fail and are dropped silently), and at least one rewritten chunk carries a `through` time past its own lines, up to the end of the stream's next chunk. Which reads lose lines then depends on the direction and on which chunk is opened first.

### Environment

- Loki 3.7.7 (`7a40404f`) and 3.7.9 (`d3b4a2f7`), official release binaries (`loki-darwin-arm64.zip`, checksums verified against the release `SHA256SUMS`).
- Single binary (`-target=all`), `auth_enabled: false`, filesystem store, `tsdb` / `v13`, 24h index period, `retention_enabled: true`, `delete_request_store: filesystem`. The full config is in the script.

items.title: AskGogo Enterprise Commerce OS — Nugget-style Tipplr × Flipkart pilot (spec / shadow first)
items.body:
## Goal
Build **AskGogo Enterprise Commerce Operations** from publicly documented Nugget patterns, piloted in **Tipplr × Flipkart food delivery**. This issue is a discovery/specification and gated implementation backlog, **not approval to mutate live restaurant/order/refund/payment systems**.

## Evidence and inspiration (public, not Nugget proprietary code)
- Nugget architecture: https://www.nugget.com/technology/ — preselected intent, approved knowledge, validated account/order context, pre-response guardrail, execution, per-session measurement; SOP→workflow builder, evals, analytics.
- Nugget Zomato case study: https://www.nugget.com/resources/zomato-case-study/ — multilingual support, photo triage, human copilot, omnichannel tickets, claimed cost and CSAT improvements. Treat all KPI figures as vendor claims.
- ONDC official specs / validation: https://github.com/ONDC-Official and https://github.com/ONDC-Official/log-validation-utility
- ONDC buyer-app grievance routing: https://www.ondc.org/pages/complaint.html
- Existing AskGogo architecture plan: docs/architecture/07-memory-scopes.md (**plan only**; founder approval required for any schema step).
- Coordinate with ongoing AskGogo engineering via #274 and AGENTS.md. Do not modify files under an active lease.

## Product definition
A tenant-scoped, outcome-led enterprise agent system for four personas:
1. Restaurant manager / Petpooja operator
2. Customer / order recipient (only through approved Flipkart or authorized buyer-app channels)
3. Delivery partner (only through authorized LSP channels)
4. Tipplr/Flipkart operations and human support

**First wedge: restaurant/store-ID mapping failure → order cancellations**. Automatically detect and safely escalate mapping drift, missing acks, duplicate orders, item outages, delayed prep/pickup, ticket escalations, reconciliation mismatches. Learn from verified fixes; never treat a bot response or HTTP 200 as completed outcome.

## Architecture / boundaries
```
Authorized channels (merchant WhatsApp, ops UI, partner support, voice later)
  -> tenant + role + subject authentication
  -> deterministic event/intent classifier + structured context resolver
  -> approved SOP/contract RAG with provenance
  -> typed workflow orchestrator and policy/approval gates
  -> provider adapters (Tipplr OMS, Petpooja POS, ONDC seller/buyer interfaces,
     Flipkart's explicitly authorized integration, logistics provider)
  -> idempotent outbox / callback reconciliation / unknown-outcome suspension
  -> pre-send validator + audited user-facing response
  -> tickets, human takeover, SLAs, per-outcome analytics
```
Use **separate enterprise tenant workspace** from consumer AskGogo; do not read personal user memory by default. RLS, org membership, scoped credentials, RBAC, event provenance, retention/privacy, per-tenant budget caps and full audit. Any schema/permissions changes require owner approval.

## Milestones (separate PRs)
**M0 Discovery (read-only):**
- Identify authoritative Tipplr order engine/repository, API contracts, Event/Webhook samples, status map and permission boundaries. Current accessible `tipplr-sales-crm` and `tipplr-sales-crm-app` appear to be sales CRM, not confirmed OMS.
- Obtain approved integration documents from Flipkart, Tipplr, Petpooja, and participating ONDC entities; never infer consumer APIs from seller docs.
- Obtain redacted failed-order samples and source-coded cancellation reason categories; establish baseline by restaurant/store/provider, 7/30 day windows.

**M1 Shadow-mode Operations Sentinel:**
- Read-only normalized `order_event`, `restaurant_mapping`, `provider_callback` and `support_ticket` feeds with dedupe; reconcile on_confirm/ack/status and POS status where authorized.
- Detect `store_id_mismatch`, `provider_ack_timeout`, `duplicate_delivery`, `menu_stock_stale`, `order_stuck` and classify `unknown` explicitly.
- Human operations dashboard with evidence, recommended action, SLA and replay.

**M2 Safe assisted resolution:**
- Merchant/ops WhatsApp text (voice later), order lookup and merchant role checks, draft ticket/resolution, manual ownership, escalations with warm summary.
- Suggested mapping corrections require operator approval; create append-only audit. Allow approved non-financial corrections only after partner contract and API verification.

**M3 Supervised automation:**
- Scoped adapters, parameter validation, rate limits, idempotency keys, concurrency/locking, callback/readback verification, DLQ/replay, exactly-once business-effect semantics as far as partner supports; suspend unknown outcome, never blind retry.
- Auto-send alerts/tickets under notification consent and quiet hours; no refunds/cancels/compensation without specific policy + approved rightsholder.

**M4 Nugget-parity platform:**
- Versioned SOP → human-reviewed DAG builder; flow drafts, policy bindings, dry-run; regression evals and simulated backends; immutable workflow publishing; Insights/Journeys (verified resolution, missed SLA, escalation, intervention, cancellation prevention).

**M5 Omnichannel voice + enterprise packaging:**
- Hindi, Kannada, Hinglish pilot and noisy/8kHz telephony tests, barge-in, warm transfer, consent & recording controls; optional languages only after testing. Tenant provisioning, SSO/RBAC, billing, data controls.

## P0 acceptance tests
1. Restaurant A's order cannot show under restaurant B / other enterprise tenant, including memory and RAG.
2. Wrong mapped Petpooja ID flagged with **evidence**, no automatic swap; human approves only validated correction.
3. Unknown/missing POS ACK remains unresolved; no fake success.
4. Duplicate webhook/callback/replay generates one logical ticket/action.
5. Out-of-order ONDC statuses remain consistent with actual domain and contract version.
6. Cancel/refund flow rejects unauthorized persona, prohibited state and invalid reason.
7. Payment/refund action never retried after timeout without provider status proof.
8. Stock stale triggers nudge not unsupported stock write.
9. Human takeover carries transcript, order context, exact attempted actions, evidence.
10. Consent/DND, redaction, opt-out, access revocation all enforced.
11. Event ingestion load/latency/durability tests at representative peak volume.
12. Verified resolution requires actual provider state transition, not ticket auto-close.
13. Every support answer cites approved versioned SOP source; contradictory policy fails closed.
14. Regression suite runs on mock partner payloads before any partner production call.
15. Support/customer notifications only to authorized recipient with policy-confirmed channel rights.

## Go/no-go KPIs
- Seller/POS mapping-related cancellations per 1,000 orders
- % orders with verified POS ack within agreed SLA
- Median/p95 time to identify and resolve mapping incident
- Verified resolution rate (not bot deflection), repeat contacts, false fixes
- Refund/cancel error rate and human override rate
- Cost per *verified* resolution, no cross-tenant leaks

## Explicit non-goals / gates
- No scraping or reverse-engineering Nugget's proprietary software; use public product patterns.
- No claims of Nugget source access or identical implementation.
- No production Flipkart/Petpooja/ONDC writes before credentials, documented contract, synthetic/staging tests, explicit permission and owner-approved release.
- No more outbound messages/voice calls without opt-in and contractual authorization.
- Do not merge/deploy anything directly from this issue or bypass #274 review/lease discipline.

## Initial output requested
Read-only inventory + API contract checklist + redacted 30-case cancellation corpus design + versioned workflow state machine + explicit acceptance/rollback plan.

items.title: Shared/Dedicated parity program: de-shim the Shared agent to data-layer unity

labels.name: needs-triage
labels.description: Open issue requires area, type, priority, and acceptance-mode triage

items.body:
## Goal

Nubs + shaw directive: eliminate every shim/divergence where the Shared agent behaves differently from a real Dedicated agent, unifying at the DATA layer (same schemas, same embedding space, same recall semantics) while keeping the edge compute model that makes the $0 tier economical. Terminal acceptance: **the same canon battery that proves nubilio green runs against a staging Shared agent and passes** — parity proven by the same probes, not by claim.

## What is already REAL (no work needed)

- Genuine `AgentRuntime` from `@elizaos/core/edge` with `runtime.initialize()` and real action planning (workerd foundation #19774/#19775)
- Real plugin contract + edge plugins: web-search, todos (tenant-Postgres state via Hyperdrive), shared-reminders (live +3:00 fire, exactly-once DO tombstone)
- Canonical turn pipeline (response handler), exactly-once egress, billing/admission chain
- Edge webhook path (#20380) + activation control (#20500), keep-warm (#20476), edge plugin contract pin (#20489)

## The divergence ledger (the honest "shim list"), in fix order

1. **Memory recall is a lexical heuristic, not memory.** `MEMORY_HINT` regex + 40-message cap (24 recent + 16 keyword-salient) stands in for semantic recall. Dedicated has memory tables + FACTS provider + embedding search. *Fix: Phases 2–3 below; the regex gets deleted, not improved.*
2. **No knowledge accumulation.** `enableRelationships: false`, no facts/entity extraction, no reflection — Shared learns nothing durable about the user. *Fix: Phase 4.*
3. **No trajectories** (`enableTrajectories: false`) — Shared turns are not debuggable the way nubilio turns are; we felt this on every staging incident. *Fix: Phase 5 (sampled).*
4. **Character projection gap** — templates/knowledge/settings surfaces unused on the cloud path (known pre-launch note). *Fix: Phase 6.*
5. **Embeddings: off / OpenAI-priced when on.** *Fix: Phase 1 (in flight — self-hosted 384d sidecar, claim at HQ 18043163).*
6. Cache-only fail-closed first turn (warming 503s) — mitigated by create-prewarm + keep-warm cron; residual acceptable but tracked.

## The phases

- **P1 — self-hosted embeddings** (bge-small-en-v1.5, 384d, TEI sidecar on Railway; force-local flag kills the OpenAI dependency). Status: claimed, building.
- **P2 — real memory tables at the edge**: Shared writes the SAME core memory schema per-tenant via Hyperdrive (generalize the todos-edge tenant-postgres pattern; plugin-sql already boots in workerd). DO stays as hot window + turn coordinator.
- **P3 — semantic recall at the edge**: embed turns fire-and-forget in `waitUntil` (zero turn latency), FACTS-style provider with keyword-miss → embedding search (#20514 pattern). Delete `MEMORY_HINT`.
- **P4 — knowledge parity**: post-turn facts/entity extraction (reflection evaluator edge port) into the same tables Dedicated uses.
- **P5 — observability parity**: sampled trajectory recording for Shared turns.
- **P6 — character parity**: templates/knowledge/settings served on the cloud path.
- **P7 — the proof**: port the nubilio canon battery to run against staging Shared; parity scoreboard maintained at HQ until green.

**Upgrade prize**: with P2–P4, Shared→Dedicated upgrade becomes a pointer flip over identical tenant rows — memory continuous from first $0 message to paid container. The cutover transplant machinery gets deleted.

## Review/ownership

Fleet claims per phase at HQ #18309. Billing-touching pieces (P1 pricing rows) → gauss + provider-truth lane. Product calls embedded: P3 turns on per-turn sidecar compute for $0 tier (cheap, not zero) — nubs/shaw sign-off noted per phase.

items.title: Full Drizzle schema + per-tenant connection
items.body:
**M1** · **deps:** #2 · **Spec:** tech-stack §2, §5.4; Brief §4, §9
**Model:** 🧠 Opus 4.8 — run `/fast` (security-critical / subtle; a silent miss here costs more than the tokens).
**⚠ Audit fix (Tier 1):** Add the 8 audit tables; **worker uses `DATABASE_URL_SESSION` (session-mode)** — transaction-mode pooling breaks pgmq/LISTEN/advisory-locks; define `content_hash` over normalized text **+ namespace**.
**🛠 Setup prerequisite (FIRST needed here):** real Supabase via the **Supabase CLI + local stack**. M0 ran hermetically on pglite, but `getDb()` + the real `DATABASE_URL` need real Supabase — and applying the migration against it here is the **second test lane** that catches pglite-vs-real divergence (pglite's pgvector ≠ Supabase's; the HNSW/extension-version trap from #2).
> **YOU do these 3 one-time, machine/account-level steps first — Claude Code can't (they need Docker + your account):**
> 1. **Install Docker Desktop** and have it *running* (the local Supabase stack runs in Docker; `supabase start` needs it).
> 2. **Install the Supabase CLI** — `brew install supabase/tap/supabase`.
> 3. **`supabase login`** — one browser click-through.
>
> After that, **Claude Code drives everything else**: `supabase start`, create/apply migrations, `db reset`, `gen types`, run the real-Supabase test lane.

(Also required by #37 Auth, #39 provisioning. Recommend doing the 3 steps a bit earlier so the real-Supabase lane exists before you need it.)
**Context.** Everything sits on this. One Postgres per client; the engine connects to exactly one tenant.
**Tasks.**
- [ ] Set up Supabase CLI + `supabase start` (local Postgres+pgvector+Auth); confirm the migration applies cleanly on it, not just pglite.
- [ ] Define all tables in `db/schema.ts`: memories(+slots), chunks, connector_schemas, connections(+trust_level), identity_map, ingestion_log, inbox_items, task_state, user_clearance, roles, system_config, traces, audit_log.
- [ ] Align columns 1:1 with `@aios/shared` types.
- [ ] `getDb()` reads `DATABASE_URL` (Supavisor-pooled); engine refuses to boot without `TENANT_ID`.
- [ ] First migration documented as expand/contract; write the migration README.
**Acceptance.**
- [ ] Schema migrates clean on a fresh Supabase project (local `supabase start` and/or cloud); `pnpm typecheck` passes with types flowing end-to-end.
- [ ] Booting without `TENANT_ID` fails fast (fail-closed).
**Out of scope.** RLS (we use physical isolation, not RLS); data seeding (#39/#43).
**Watch.** Connection-pool gotchas with pgmq — verify LISTEN/advisory-lock behaviour under Supavisor transaction mode.

---

items.title: [F2-18][P3/P6] renox-gateway + renox-template: `Renox-Request-Id` on every response, `/__renox/events` ingestion with limits, CSP `report-to`, platform client script served with nonce

milestone.title: F2 SSR and templates
milestone.description: Transpiler, renderer with fuel, loaders/actions, htmx fragments. Done: shop example runs; D7 decided by B8.

items.body:
## Context
Contract #125. The gateway (#22) is the right place to receive browser events: same origin as the app, tenant id already known from routing, limits already enforced per tenant, log sink already attached (#28, #55). The template engine (#38, #40) emits the page shell and is where the script tag, the nonce, and the `<meta name="renox-request-id">` belong.

## Goal
Every response carries `Renox-Request-Id`; pages include `<script nonce="…" src="/__renox/client.js">` and the request-id meta tag; the CSP from #47 carries `report-to`; `/__renox/events` validates, limits, normalises, and writes events to the tenant's log sink as structured log lines with `source=client`; the dev worker forwards the same events to the CLI's dev channel.

## Scope
In:
- `crates/renox-gateway/src/request_id.rs`: id generated at the gateway (already used for logs), set on every response including 4xx/5xx and static.
- `crates/renox-gateway/src/client_events.rs`: route `/__renox/events` (POST only, `204` always), body cap 32 KB, token buckets per IP and per tenant from the contract, JSON Schema validation (`jsonschema` crate) or CSP report normalisation, truncation, then `log::client_event(tenant, deployment, event)`; metrics `client_events_total{kind}` and `client_events_dropped_total{reason}`; the endpoint never touches the isolate.
- `/__renox/client.js`: served from the gateway with a content hash in `ETag`, `Cache-Control: immutable`, the file embedded at build time from `sdk/client/dist/` (the file is built by #127; until then an empty stub ships).
- `renox-template`: page shell emits the script tag with the request nonce (#47) and `<meta name="renox-request-id" content="…">`; fragments do not (they get the id from the header).
- CSP (#47): add `report-to renox` with a `Reporting-Endpoints: renox="/__renox/events?kind=csp"` header and `report-uri` for older browsers; `report-only` mode supported through `[security.csp] report_only = true`.
- Dev mode: the worker exposes the events on the dev SSE channel the CLI subscribes to (#43) so the overlay can show them.
- Tests: header present on every response kind; oversized body → 204 and dropped metric; rate limit → 204 and dropped; valid batch → log lines with `tenant_id`, `source=client`, `kind`; CSP report body normalised; events endpoint disabled when `[client] events = false`.
Out: the client script itself (#127), dashboard and sourcemaps (#128).

## Steps
1. Request id on every response path (including the static and error paths).
2. Events route with limits, validation, normalisation, log sink write.
3. Script serving and template shell changes; CSP reporting headers.
4. Dev channel forwarding.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] All tests above pass; no `CellDispatcher` call for `/__renox/*` (fake dispatcher assertion).
- [ ] `shop` page HTML contains the nonce'd script tag and the meta tag; `renox check --security` shows the reporting headers.
- [ ] Events appear in the tenant log file with `source=client` within one batch interval.

## Dependencies
Blocked by: #125, #40, #47, #43. Blocks: #127, #128.

## Files
Owned: `crates/renox-gateway/src/request_id.rs`, `src/client_events.rs`, `src/client_script.rs`, `tests/client_events.rs`, `crates/renox-template/src/shell.rs` (script and meta emission), `crates/renox-gateway/src/security/csp.rs` (reporting directives).

## Branch
`r/f2-18-client-events-gateway`

## Gate F1 notes (#37)
- #22 is closed and dropped; #43 (the `renox dev` proxy) added. Not parallel-safe any more (label removed).
- The request-id work is done (`x-renox-request-id`): reduce it to tests that 429/431/413/503/static/404 all carry the header.
- The gateway has no log sink: a `ClientEventSink` trait implemented by `renox-cell` through the runtime's `RedactingSink`.
- Metrics: use `Gateway::stats` counters; Prometheus is #77.
- Commit the built `client.js` under `crates/renox-gateway/assets/`, with a CI check, so a Rust build does not need Bun. Dev: intercept `/__renox/events` in the `renox dev` proxy.

items.title: Track Engram → Spanner compatibility execution and sign-off
items.body:
## Current scope decision — 2026-10-08: disposable experiments

Stakeholder explicitly excludes historical-data migration, old-pack identity conversion and cross-version historical upgrade work from ALL current goals. Do not spend analysis/implementation/review effort on migration or treat it as a completion blocker. Focus on actual Engram ingestion, ontology projection and retrieval on real Spanner using disposable data. In-run revision history and same-pack retry/recovery remain covered. Existing migration-only scenarios/tickets stay deferred, never falsely passed or closed. Goal Three is still unstarted pending approval.

Persisted goal-wide scope and verification standard: https://github.com/arunmenon/Engram/blob/9294db7/docs/review/spanner-compatibility/2026-10-08-small-goal-inventory.md . This scope decision overrides historical migration acceptance text below for current goal execution.

---

## Current agreed context — 2026-10-07

**Scope:** Real-Spanner compatibility remains unsigned: baseline 65 rows is separate from planned composition/tenant extensions and feature acceptance.

**Required proof:** Maintain all scenario assertions, publish redacted evidence, resolve failures/partial/blockers and verify tenant-bound handshake, ingestion, workers, both retrieval paths and operations.

**Shared decisions:** Core is mandatory. Optional memory/user/domain capabilities compose through declared dependencies, without pairwise hardcoded flows. Authenticated tenant identity resolves its authorized Spanner database and pack bundle; processing and retrieval use that same context. Never infer authorization from agent_id, caller-chosen database or artifact IDs.

**Tracking and status:** Parent #34 holds the reconciled six-bucket scope; #35/#42 own composition/capability controls, #43 tenant routing, #39 exact conformance and #41 real-Spanner execution. This is a scope/context reconciliation, not a fresh runtime verification. The issue remains open; historical reproductions below retain their original revision, backend and run scope. Historical memory probes are diagnostic evidence, not cloud acceptance. No Redis/Neo4j runners or cross-backend migration are required. Pinned documentation links below are historical published snapshots; newer local reports/run artifacts remain unpublished unless explicitly linked to a published revision.

---

Track Engram’s end-to-end compatibility with real Google Cloud Spanner. This is the execution and sign-off umbrella; #34 owns reusable ontology-pack integration and its implementation slices. Existing defects remain linked rather than duplicated or reparented.

## Baseline and evidence

Current baseline: **65 scenarios: 14 passed, 36 failed, 13 not fully executed, 2 blocked. No compatibility sign-off.** `not_run` includes partial execution whose complete assertions remain open. These are scenario counts, not unique defect counts. The 36 failed scenarios map to existing defects across #4–#33; local fixes and scoped reviews do not close cloud scenarios without reruns.

- [Scenario matrix](https://github.com/arunmenon/Engram/blob/5e9c883/docs/review/spanner-compatibility/scenarios.csv)
- [Execution ledger](https://github.com/arunmenon/Engram/blob/5e9c883/docs/review/spanner-compatibility/runs.jsonl)
- [Findings](https://github.com/arunmenon/Engram/blob/5e9c883/docs/review/spanner-compatibility/findings.md)
- [Compatibility and implementation plan](https://github.com/arunmenon/Engram/blob/5e9c883/docs/review/2026-10-06-spanner-compatibility-plan.md)

The published links are immutable baseline snapshots. Current working records live at the same repository paths. Raw `runs/` artifacts are currently local and unpublished; a recorded evidence path is not a public artifact link. Publish reviewable, redacted evidence before final sign-off.

## Execution rules

- Exercise Engram APIs, workers, admin tools and retrieval against real Spanner. No Redis or Neo4j runners; memory tests cannot substitute for cloud acceptance.
- Track every run in the execution ledger before starting. Record scenario IDs, source revision and working diff, configuration, resource scope, observations, linked defects, cleanup and final outcomes. Keep credentials out of evidence.
- Use the authorized disposable databases `engram` and `engram-compat-target` on `portiq-mvp/engram-experiment`; preserve databases and schema. Serialize destructive fixture resets and record their scope.
- Classify failures as shared Engram engine, Engram Spanner adapter, test harness or environment. Link each confirmed product defect and rerun affected scenarios after fixes.
- Test ontology updates and rebuilt-graph cutover within Spanner while preserving the ledger. Redis-to-Spanner migration is outside scope.
- Keep this checklist and the CSV synchronized. Check a scenario only when all its listed assertions have passed. Track partial assertions in subchecks; do not promote partial results to passes.

- [x] **ART-05** — evaluation/combined packs; `ontology evaluate → artifact API`. Verify: pending TTL/read failure; explicit intent409; PDLC+CRM; namespace and weight composition. Defects: none recorded. Latest run: `20261006-cloud-coverage-reconciliation-08`.

- [x] **USER-02** — delete; `DELETE /v1/users/{user_id}`. Verify: owned nodes/edges deleted; other user/shared nodes and unrelated evidence preserved. Defects: none recorded. Latest run: `20261006-cloud-coverage-reconciliation-06`.
- [x] **FB-01** — feedback; `POST /v1/feedback`. Verify: audit event + clamp/helpful/irrelevant; missing and repeated node IDs; resubmission. Defects: none recorded. Latest run: `20261006-cloud-coverage-reconciliation-06`.
- [x] **ONT-01** — inspect/evaluate; `GET /v1/ontology + ontology CLI`. Verify: status/evaluate record/no record; missing/failing eval sets; pending state. Defects: none recorded. Latest run: `20261006-cloud-coverage-reconciliation-08`.
- [x] **LIFE-02** — archive; `consolidation + supported archive/replay entry`. Verify: FS then GCS if deployment configured; archive failure preserves docs; restore path/recovery proof. Defects: none recorded. Latest run: `20261006-cloud-coverage-reconciliation-08`.
- [x] **APP-03** — CRM journey; `import API → projection → artifact API`. Verify: accounts/contacts/deals/current lifecycle/coverage evidence. Defects: none recorded. Latest run: `20261006-cloud-coverage-reconciliation-04`.
- [x] **APP-04** — combined journey; `ingress → workers → artifact/memory APIs`. Verify: PDLC and CRM active together; pack independence and shared core. Defects: none recorded. Latest run: `20261006-cloud-coverage-reconciliation-04`.

## Blockers and scope extensions

- BOOT-02: ordinary ADC and the full credential-failure matrix remain unproven; an explicit one-hour token bootstrap does not prove ADC behavior.
- APP-06: obtain actual Keymaker inputs, expected questions and provenance requirements before app sign-off.
- #34 and #35–#39 add reusable contracts/capabilities, projection semantics, duplicate identity, processing outcomes and conformance. #40 adds agreed PDLC journeys. #42 adds optional built-in processing/retrieval with mandatory core; #43 adds authenticated database-per-tenant routing and isolation. Explicit acceptance extensions COMP-01–06 and TEN-01–03 are planned, not executed; preserve the 65-row baseline separately.
- Add explicit versioned scenario rows for those extensions before execution; preserve the 65-row baseline and show the added denominator separately. Cover the complete PDLC event inventory, CRM and an unfamiliar pack, including coexistence, rather than treating one successful PR example as pack conformance.

## Completion criteria

- [ ] All baseline assertions pass through Engram on real Spanner, including previously failed, partial and blocked scenarios; no silent exclusions.
- [ ] Agreed #34/#40 acceptance extensions have explicit expected artifacts, relationships, versions, evidence and retrieval answers, and pass on Spanner.
- [ ] Failure/recovery, retries, duplicates/conflicts, ordering, concurrency, pagination, deadlines, retention, replay and upgrades are exercised wherever applicable in the matrix and feature acceptance.
- [ ] Every confirmed defect has a linked disposition and a passing cloud regression; local-only fixes remain identified until verified.
- [ ] Run ledger, checklist, matrix and issue statuses agree; redacted evidence is published and independently reviewable.
- [ ] Final review records residual limitations explicitly. Any proposed scope exception requires an explicit decision and does not count as a passing scenario.

This umbrella remains open until these acceptance criteria are satisfied. It does not assert Spanner compatibility today.


## Entity-only native ANN follow-up (#44)

Track #44: the Engram Spanner adapter currently searches embeddings across all GraphNodes and returns those IDs as Entity IDs. This is a source-confirmed integration defect, not an executed cloud failure or a Spanner service bug. Repair must restrict the ANN corpus before top-k, preserve stored embeddings, validate schema/index readiness, and pass real Engram→Spanner differential tests with inactive/non-Entity vectors and colliding IDs. Local post-filtering is insufficient. Baseline scenario status remains unchanged until registered cloud reruns prove acceptance.

items.title: Tracking: move multitenancy from sharded (one process per collection, per-tenant tables and shard keys) to non-sharded (shared structures served by any process)

labels.name: refactor
labels.description: Code refactoring that doesn't add new features.

labels.name: keep-open
labels.description: Prevents the auto-close task from closing this issue.

labels.name: horizontal scaling
labels.description: Wrong or unsafe when more than one server process serves the same backends (replicas or workers)

items.body:
### Where to start (status 2026-10-02)

**Storage layer.** Segment store: done (#1661 on main). Qdrant and Milvus: #1733 -> #1734 -> #1735 -> #1736 in review (SQL collection registry, an incarnation per collection life, fenced handles, claimed purge); they close #1524, #1525 and #1563 on merge. SQLite stores: #1536 stays with the SQLite store fixes (#1460 to #1675), and they are HOST or PROCESS scope by declaration (#1757).

**Above the stores**, in priority order. Each is a tracking issue with a one-glance table (what is wrong, best fix, order) and a PR split, and each child issue shows its tracker at the top.

1. #1755 Session lifecycle: the `sessions` row as registry plus durable jobs. Tracks #1543, #1571, #1575, #1576, #1577, #1600, #1655, #1728, #1749.
2. #1756 Background work: one claimable-job primitive for provision, delete, ingestion and purge. Tracks #1745, #1749, #1699, #1738, #1722.
3. #1757 Concurrency scope per component, so declarative memory and short-term memory stay available for single-replica deployments without a routing layer. Tracks #1748, #1753, #1745.
3. #1758 Replica-safe defaults in one change. Tracks #1746, #1747, #1730, #1750, #1751, #1752, #1754.

Design reference: #1579 (deferred as a whole; its vocabulary and target shapes are what the tracking issues cite).

**Labels.** `horizontal scaling`: wrong or unsafe with more than one server process on the same backends. `concurrency`: wrong under concurrent requests or processes regardless of replica count (races, lost updates, unarbitrated read-then-write). `recovery`: a failure or crash leaves durable state nothing repairs (partial writes, lost jobs, no retry or terminal state). An issue carries every label that applies.

### Why this issue exists

The issues linked below were filed one at a time, most of them as bugs. Read individually they look like an accumulation of unrelated defects in the storage layer. Read together they are one change of model: the codebase was built for **sharded** horizontal scaling (each logical collection or partition owned by exactly one process, and separated from other tenants by a physical structure of its own), and the requirement is now **non-sharded** scaling (any process serves any tenant, and tenants are rows or values inside structures they share). This issue states that change once, records why the previous model was there, classifies each linked issue against it, and tracks what remains.

### The model the codebase was built on, and why

Two decisions, both explicit and documented when they were made.

**1. Ownership by process sharding.** #1201 (merged 2026-04-02) set the `VectorStore` contract that is still in `common/vector_store/vector_store.py` today:

> A given logical collection identified by a (namespace, name) pair must be managed by at most one process at a time. The consumer is responsible for sharding names across processes.

Its description states the guarantees plainly: "safe concurrent usage on a single process" and "safe concurrent sharded usage (one node per logical collection) on multiple processes". With ownership fixed per process, lifecycle operations (create, open-or-create, delete) could be read-check-write sequences guarded by per-process `asyncio` locks, and backends without transactions or unique constraints (Qdrant, Milvus) could keep their catalog of logical collections inside the backend itself. The multi-process guarantee was correct under its contract and was never broken: strict sharding always worked. The restriction itself is what became the limitation (#1524, #1525).

**2. Per-tenant physical structures.** #1205 (merged 2026-05-08) scoped the event memory "by partition key: should allow sharding and horizontal scaling", and on PostgreSQL gave every segment-store partition its own pair of child tables under LIST-partitioned parents, created and dropped by per-tenant DDL. #1292 (merged 2026-05-02) gave every SQLite vector collection its own tables, for a stated reason: "Partition keys are avoided in favor of per-collection tables, since sqlite-vec ANN indexes may not support them." Qdrant's `is_distributed` flag gives every logical collection its own shard key. The payoff was real: deleting a tenant was one `DROP` rather than a row-scanning `DELETE`, one tenant's rows never interleaved with another's in a heap or index, and backend index limitations were sidestepped. Note that #1201 already rejected one native collection per tenant ("most vector databases recommend against one collection per tenant, and empirical tests show that many collections induces significant overhead"); the per-tenant structure was the shard key or child table beneath a shared native collection, not the collection itself.

Both decisions fit the deployments they served: a single server process, embedded SQLite as a first-class backend, an opt-in pre-GA event backend, and tenant counts at which per-tenant DDL was cheap. Nothing below should be read as those decisions having been mistakes at the time.

### What changed

Two requirements the sharded model does not meet:

- **Multiple server processes must serve the same tenants.** Any replica handles any session; routing by session affinity is not a requirement a hosted deployment can carry. This is the horizontal-scalability problem as restated in #1524 and #1525: multiple processes working the *same* collections and partitions, not more processes each owning their own.
- **Tenant counts of tens of thousands to millions**, with individual tenants ranging from tens of thousands to tens of millions of rows (`design/segment_store_shared_tables.md` in #1545).

### Why the sharded model fails them

Measured, in the linked issues and in the design doc:

| Cost of the model | Evidence |
| --- | --- |
| Per-tenant DDL on shared PostgreSQL parents | #1544's second half, and the design doc in #1545: create and delete DDL deadlocked with writers and with each other, on upstream and on every intermediate fix, in two cycle shapes; the class has nowhere to live once there is no lifecycle DDL. (#1544's first half, a `CASCADE` that removed the shared foreign key, is a plain bug; see the classification below.) |
| Per-tenant partitions and prepared statements | #1546: after five executions PostgreSQL switches to a generic plan that locks every child partition per read: 9 locks per read with a custom plan, 319 with the generic plan at 316 partitions, HTTP 500 `out of shared memory` at 128-way concurrency. Each per-tenant table also costs about 5 catalog relations and disk files, which does not survive the required tenant counts. |
| Per-tenant shard keys on Qdrant | #1564: 450 ms per tenant admission, 45 s for 100 tenants against 0.3 s with payload partitioning, 505 segments against 5, and cluster mode required. |
| Per-process ownership | #1524, #1525: the moment two processes manage the same name, lock-guarded read-check-write lifecycle has no arbiter. #1566 (folded into #1564): the in-process lock table was a leftover of that serialisation. |

The comparison that settled the segment store (raw asyncpg, 40 tenants x 2000 row-pairs, pgvector:pg16, 2 CPUs; full table in the design doc):

| layout | ingest | seed read | tenant create | catalog cost |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `PARTITION OF` children | 8.7-9.2k pairs/s | 0.43-0.46 ms | ~12 ms DDL | ~5 relations/tenant |
| shared tables | 15k pairs/s | 0.21 ms | 0.006 ms | none |

Per-tenant tables won only small-tenant removal latency (9 ms drop against 58 ms row delete), which does not justify their catalog cost at the required tenant counts. This is the industry's pool model: O(1) logical deletion via a registry plus asynchronous batched reclamation; O(1) physical drops exist only in per-tenant-resource (silo) architectures, which the tenant-count requirement excludes.

### The target model

The layer above the stores that ties these together (a tenant record with a step table and a reconciler, UUID-only store keys minted per tenant lifetime, a single tenant handle, and prompt purge as best-effort) is proposed in `design/tenant_lifecycle.md` under #1579, with the resource-level contracts the stores expose to it. The bullets below are the store-level targets that proposal builds on.

- **A tenant is a row, not a relation.** One registry row per live tenant, carrying a random `incarnation` minted at creation; data rows and records are keyed by the incarnation. Creating a tenant is an insert.
- **One physical structure per backend, shared by every tenant**: shared tables on SQL; payload-partitioned native collections on vector backends, with native collections shared by config as #1201 already did.
- **Lifecycle arbitrated by the database, so any process may perform it**: unique constraints decide create races, row locks serialise delete against in-flight writers, `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` lets concurrent purgers split a backlog.
- **Deletion is O(1) logical** (registry delete plus a purge-queue entry in one transaction); **physical reclamation is asynchronous**, bounded per call, safe to run from any process, and driven by a background purger.
- **Stale handles cannot reach a successor.** A handle carries the incarnation it was opened on. Where the backend can pin a registry row (the segment store, with `FOR SHARE`), a stale handle raises; where it cannot (the vector backends), a stale handle's writes land in a dead incarnation that nothing reads and reclamation removes, with lease validation against the registry as the remaining option (#1563, #1564). Either way a tenant recreated under the same key is unreachable from the old handle, on any process, without coordination.
- **The contract says what each store supports.** The blanket "at most one process" sentence goes; a store whose metadata moves to a cross-process authority says so, and a deployment can introspect what it may do instead of relying on out-of-band knowledge (#1524, #1525).
- **Native containers are provisioned, not created on the request path.** Creating a logical collection is one registry insert arbitrated by a primary key; the container it lands in already exists, shaped once per deployment (one schema per container, because a shared container cannot carry per-tenant schemas) and ensured by the same provisioning step that owns SQL schema (#1572, #1573, #1570).
- **Per-tenant physical isolation stays available as a tier** for an oversized tenant (Qdrant's tiered multitenancy, per #1564), never as the default.

### Status by component

Each row names the issues that carry the work; fixes and their state are tracked on those issues, not here.

| Component | Sharded model | Target | Issues |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Segment store, PostgreSQL | LIST-partitioned parents, per-tenant child tables and DDL | shared tables keyed by incarnation; registry and purge queue; writers pin the registry row | #1544, #1546, #1549 |
| Segment store, SQLite | shared tables keyed by partition key (never sharded), no fencing | same architecture on every dialect | #1549 |
| Vector store lifecycle, all backends | per-backend ad-hoc catalogs, per-process locks; contract forbids multi-process management | collection metadata arbitrated by a cross-process authority, so any process can create, open and delete; the contract states what each store supports | #1524, #1525 |
| Vector store create path and interface | native container created inside `create_collection` (a dual write across registry and backend, safe only because names are content-addressed); per-collection `VectorStoreCollectionConfig` promising per-tenant schemas | containers provisioned before serving; `create_collection` is a registry insert; collection shape configured per deployment | #1572, #1573 |
| Qdrant | `is_distributed` shard key per logical collection; native name re-derived from `sha256(config)` on every open; in-process lock table | payload partitioning; native name pinned at creation; lifecycle arbitrated by the cross-process authority; reclamation of dead partition keys | #1564, #1565, #1563, #1562 (#1566 folded into #1564) |
| SQLite vector stores | per-collection tables; stale handles reach the successor | incarnation-scoped native resources (per-collection tables stay; the store's stated reason is that sqlite-vec's index may not support a partition key) | #1536 |
| Milvus | per-record `partition_key` field filtered on queries (already value-based); catalog in a dummy-vector `__registry` collection | catalog moved to the cross-process authority | #1524, #1535 |
| Session data manager | read-then-write on session rows, safe only with one process per session | database-arbitrated create and update | #1543 |
| Schema provisioning | every process runs `create_all` at boot; no migration path for a layout change | one provisioning owner; migrations carry layout changes such as the segment store's | #1570 |
| Above the stores | process-local handle caches; no domain-error-to-status mapping | evict and re-resolve on a stale handle; explicit API status | #1571 |

Found along the way, not sharding-related, but blocking correctness on SQLite: #1568 (per-connection state registered per store on caller-supplied engines) and #1542 (engines built without WAL, busy timeout, or explicit write transactions). Contract issues that matter more once native collections are shared across tenants: #1534 (unbounded property-key cardinality, undeclared-property mandate) and #1535 (`indexed_properties_schema` is part of collection identity); #1573 narrows that to whether per-collection configuration belongs in the interface at all.

### How to read the linked issues

- **Plain defects, unrelated to the model**: #1544's first half (a `CASCADE` that removes a shared constraint), #1562 (config serialisation repoints data), #1568 (per-connection SQLite state registered late).
- **Handle bugs the sharded model could have fixed locally**: #1536, #1549, #1563. Each reproduces inside one process: an in-flight request holds a handle while that same process deletes and recreates the collection, and the handle reaches the successor. Real under any model, but not a failure of sharding: the owning process performs the delete and could invalidate every handle it issued at that moment, in memory. The target model removes that option, since the deleter may be another process, so invalidation moves into the data as the incarnation.
- **Costs of the sharded model that only surface at scale**: #1546, #1564, #1544's second half (lifecycle DDL deadlocking against shared parents), #1566 (in-process lifecycle serialisation), and the catalog cost per tenant. Not coding errors; the model's own behaviour under tenant counts and process counts it was not designed for.
- **Capability gaps the sharded model never had to fill**: #1524, #1525 (cross-process lifecycle arbitration), #1565 (reclamation, since a value cannot be dropped), #1543 (lost updates once two processes share a session), #1570 (a schema owner, once tenant metadata is rows and only the fixed boot-time schema is left), #1572 (a provisioning owner for native containers, once creating a collection is a registry insert).
- **Consequences of the target model**: #1571 (fencing makes staleness recognisable, so the layers above must handle it), #1573 (a shared container carries one schema, so the interface must stop promising one per collection), the asynchronous-erasure semantics (a deleted tenant is unreachable immediately and erased in the background, so synchronous erasure is a deployment's explicit choice).

### Done when

- The "at most one process" clause is gone from `vector_store.py`, replaced by a scope every store declares and honours.
- No backend creates a per-tenant physical structure by default; tenant creation is a row write everywhere, and the per-tenant tier is an explicit opt-in.
- Every lifecycle operation is safe from any process on the same backend: create races resolve by constraint, delete is idempotent and fences in-flight writers, purge is concurrent-safe and bounded.
- A stale handle cannot reach a successor tenant on any backend (raising where the backend can pin a registry row, landing in a dead incarnation where it cannot), and every backend has reclamation for dead tenants.
- Native containers are provisioned before serving and creating a logical collection is a single registry insert; collection shape is configured per deployment, one schema per container.
- Existing deployments have a stated path for each layout change: a migration through #1570's infrastructure, or an explicit recreate-schema statement of the kind the segment store overhaul makes for the pre-GA event backend.

### Out of scope

- The declarative (Neo4j and Nebula) backend: audited 2026-10-02 (#1753); kept for single-replica deployments by scope declaration (#1757), not made to scale.
- Cross-replica coherence of the process-local `EpisodicMemoryManager` cache: moved into #1755 (step 5, instances hold no per-session state once short-term memory is process-scoped, #1757). #1297, which rated it the main scaling bottleneck, is closed.

*Investigated and written by Claude (Claude Code), filed from the account of the user who commissioned the investigation.*

items.title: KF-RD-GENAI-STACK-2026-001 — Converged AI systems R&D
items.body:
# KF-RD-GENAI-STACK-2026-001

## Purpose
Durable research ledger for the methodical dissection of the 2026 GenAI stack and adjacent systems, followed by scientific/work-domain parallelisation and whole-system convergence into KEYFLOWOS / KEY.

This is **research and architectural memory**, not implementation authority. Production code remains untouched until findings are converged, dependency-ordered, and separately authorized for implementation.

## Required method for every subject
1. Technical dissection: architecture, primitives, algorithms, APIs, state, persistence, execution lifecycle, concurrency, failure/retry/cancellation, security, tenancy, observability, evaluation, scaling, latency, cost, DX, extensibility, licensing, known failure modes.
2. Source inspection where code is open.
3. Microscopic comparison against live KEYFLOWOS.
4. Scientific parallelisation: neuroscience, physiology, cybernetics/control theory, information theory, graph theory, distributed systems, statistics, OR, ecology/evolution, safety engineering, etc., but only where the mechanism is structurally transferable.
5. Work/operational parallelisation: medicine, aviation, finance/accounting, logistics, industrial safety, incident response, organizations, command-and-control, etc.
6. Mechanism extraction.
7. KEY/KEYFLOWOS hypothesis.
8. Experiment + measurable proof obligation.
9. Disposition: ADOPT / ADAPT / ABSORB / MERGE / REPLACE / REMOVE / BENCHMARK / WATCH / REJECT.
10. Hold findings for convergence; do not cargo-cult dependencies.

## Dual targets
Every useful finding is assessed for:
- KEY / KEYFLOWOS runtime.
- The autonomous development machinery building KEYFLOWOS (Claude Code / control plane / repo intelligence / review loops).

## Completion standard
The programme is not complete until individual subjects are researched, cross-domain mechanisms extracted, contradictions/duplicates identified, uncertain claims experimentally resolved, and the results converged into a small set of canonical architectural primitives with explicit invariants and proof obligations.

## Inventory
Layer 1: OpenAI/GPT; Anthropic/Claude; Gemini; Llama; DeepSeek; Qwen.
Layer 2: vLLM; Ollama; llama.cpp; Groq; Bedrock; Vertex AI.
Layer 3: LangChain; LangGraph; LlamaIndex; CrewAI; AutoGen; Pydantic AI.
Layer 4: OpenAI embeddings; Cohere; Voyage; Jina; BGE; Nomic.
Layer 5: Pinecone; Qdrant; Weaviate; Milvus; Chroma; pgvector.
Layer 6: Hugging Face; PEFT/LoRA; Unsloth; Axolotl; TRL; LLaMA-Factory.
Layer 7: DSPy; Instructor; Outlines; Guidance; BAML; provider structured outputs.
Layer 8: MCP; native function calling; A2A; computer/browser use; Composio; Arcade.
Layer 9: LangSmith; Langfuse; Ragas; DeepEval; Phoenix; W&B Weave.
Layer 10: NeMo Guardrails; Guardrails AI; Llama Guard; Lakera; Presidio; Rebuff.

The inventory expands when adjacent/superior systems are discovered.

## Progress
- R&D-01A OpenAI/GPT: first-pass technical dissection completed; findings held for Layer-1 convergence.
- R&D-01B Anthropic/Claude: active.

## R&D-01A — OpenAI/GPT holding findings
- Capability-based cognitive scheduling instead of model-name routing.
- Responses-style typed cognitive event streams should map underneath KEY's own lifecycle, not replace Cortex.
- Model tool selection is evidence/intent, never business-action authority.
- Machine-facing outputs should be schema-first; human presentation should not be reparsed into state.
- Hierarchical/deferred capability discovery ("capability paging") is high-value for KEY's large tool/connector surface.
- Prompt/context layout should be designed for cache locality: stable constitution -> stable business context -> semi-stable genome/session -> dynamic turn.
- Provider conversation state is ephemeral execution state, never canonical KEY memory.
- Classify AI work as realtime / interactive / background / batch / scheduled / event-triggered.
- Create a capability/lifecycle-aware model catalog.
- Current live repo gap: OpenAI path still uses Chat Completions and direct OpenAI calls exist outside the model gateway (embeddings/vision/voice/document paths); provider boundary is not yet fully converged.

## Continuity rule
Each completed subject should add a durable comment here containing:
- source-backed findings,
- current KEYFLOWOS comparison,
- science/work parallels,
- extracted mechanisms,
- candidate experiments,
- disposition,
- interactions/contradictions with earlier findings,
- implementation implications held for convergence.

At each layer boundary, publish a layer-convergence comment before proceeding to the next layer.

items.title: SignalDB should support ingesting entities
items.body:
## Entity Support Implementation Plan

**Scope**: Full entity support leveraging SignalDB's relational model and multi-tenant architecture. Entities represent infrastructure components, services, and resources that generate or are referenced by observability signals.

---

## Overview

OpenTelemetry Entities represent infrastructure components and services:
- Databases (`postgres-prod-01`, `redis-cache-002`)
- Message queues (`kafka-orders-topic`, `rabbitmq-payments`)
- External services (`payment-gateway-v2`, `auth-service`)
- Infrastructure (`k8s-cluster-prod-us-east`, `ec2-i-12345`)

Entities enable questions like:
- "Which services connect to `postgres-prod-01`?"
- "Show me all traces involving payment-gateway-v2"
- "What's the health/performance of services using this Kafka topic?"

---

## Implementation Phases

### Phase 1: Entity References in Resources

**Status**: Proto field exists (OpenTelemetry 0.31) but not persisted

**Current State**:
- `entity_refs` field added to Resource struct
- Currently set to `vec![]` throughout codebase
- No storage or query support

**Tasks**:
- [ ] Update Arrow schema to include `entity_refs` column in traces/logs/metrics tables
- [ ] Store entity_refs from incoming OTLP data
- [ ] Add entity_refs to Iceberg table schemas
- [ ] Verify entity_refs are preserved through write path

**Schema Change**:
```rust
// Add to traces/logs/metrics Arrow schemas
Field::new("entity_refs", DataType::Utf8, true) // JSON-encoded array
```

---

### Phase 2: Entity Table & Ingestion

**Goal**: Store entities as first-class signals alongside traces/logs/metrics

**Iceberg Table Schema**: `entities` (per tenant/dataset)
```sql
CREATE TABLE {tenant_slug}.{dataset_slug}.entities (
  entity_id STRING NOT NULL,
  entity_type STRING NOT NULL,
  entity_name STRING,
  entity_namespace STRING,
  attributes STRING,                   -- JSON map
  first_seen_time_unix_nano BIGINT,
  last_seen_time_unix_nano BIGINT,
  tenant_id STRING NOT NULL,
  dataset_id STRING NOT NULL,
  schema_version INT DEFAULT 1
)
PARTITIONED BY (entity_type, days(first_seen_time_unix_nano))
```

**OTLP Ingestion**:
- [ ] Add `POST /v1/entities` endpoint to acceptor (HTTP & gRPC)
- [ ] Create `EntityHandler` in acceptor
- [ ] Define OTLP entity proto messages
- [ ] Implement entity-to-Arrow conversion
- [ ] Add entity WAL operations

**Files to Create**:
- `src/acceptor/src/handler/otlp_entity_handler.rs`
- `src/acceptor/src/services/otlp_entity_service.rs`
- `src/common/src/flight/conversion/conversion_entities.rs`
- `src/common/src/flight/schema.rs` (add entity schema)
- `src/common/src/wal/mod.rs` (add `WalOperation::Entity`)

---

### Phase 3: Entity Query Support

**SQL Queries**:
```sql
-- List all entities of a type
SELECT entity_id, entity_name, attributes
FROM entities
WHERE entity_type = 'database'

-- Find entities by attribute
SELECT entity_id, entity_name
FROM entities
WHERE JSON_EXTRACT(attributes, '$.version') = 'PostgreSQL 15'
```

**Tasks**:
- [ ] Add entity query support to querier
- [ ] Implement `get_entities` Flight ticket
- [ ] Add entity filtering/pagination
- [ ] Add entity endpoints to router

---

### Phase 4: Entity-Signal Correlation

**Goal**: Query relationships between entities and signals

**Correlation Queries**:
```sql
-- Find all traces that reference a specific entity
SELECT t.trace_id, t.service_name, t.start_time
FROM traces t
WHERE JSON_CONTAINS(t.entity_refs, '{"entity_id": "postgres-prod-01"}')

-- Service dependency graph
SELECT DISTINCT
  source.service_name,
  target.entity_id,
  target.entity_type
FROM traces source
CROSS JOIN UNNEST(JSON_EXTRACT_ARRAY(source.entity_refs)) as entity_ref
JOIN entities target ON target.entity_id = JSON_EXTRACT_SCALAR(entity_ref, '$.entity_id')
```

**Tasks**:
- [ ] Create `ENTITY_REFS_CONTAINS()` SQL function
- [ ] Optimize JSON queries with entity_refs
- [ ] Add cross-signal entity analysis queries

---

### Phase 5: Entity Discovery & Auto-Population

**Goal**: Automatically discover and create entity records from signal data

**Entity Extraction**:
- Extract from resource attributes (database hosts, service names)
- Extract from trace attributes (external services)
- Extract from metric labels (infrastructure)

**Tasks**:
- [ ] Implement entity extraction from signals
- [ ] Add entity upsert logic (update last_seen_time)
- [ ] Make discovery opt-in/configurable

---

## Why This Fits SignalDB's Relational Model

1. **Natural Schema**: Entities map cleanly to Iceberg tables
2. **Efficient Joins**: SQL joins between entities and signals with columnar storage
3. **Partitioning**: Entity type and time-based partitioning
4. **Multi-Tenancy**: Entity isolation follows tenant/dataset model
5. **Query Power**: Complex correlation queries via SQL/DataFusion

---

## Testing

- [ ] Unit tests for entity proto conversion
- [ ] Integration tests for entity ingestion
- [ ] Query tests for entity-signal correlation
- [ ] Performance tests for large entity sets
- [ ] Multi-tenant isolation tests

---

## Documentation

- [ ] Add entity schema to flight-schemas skill
- [ ] Document entity ingestion in CLAUDE.md
- [ ] Add entity query examples
- [ ] Update architecture documentation

---

## Estimated Effort

- Phase 1: 2-3 days
- Phase 2: 5-7 days
- Phase 3: 3-4 days
- Phase 4: 2-3 days
- Phase 5: 5-7 days

**Total**: ~3-4 weeks for full implementation

---

## Related Issues

- Part of observability completeness alongside #343 (Profiles)
- Complements #412 (Cross-Signal Pivot Infrastructure)
- Enables advanced correlation features

---

**Original Context**: Proto came in with #262 (OpenTelemetry 0.31 upgrade)

items.title: Feature: tenant-bound Spanner database routing and composed pack activation
items.body:
### 2026-10-14 accepted tenant-isolation checkpoint

Public authenticated dispatch plus two pinned Spanner databases and 10 workers is verified for Core+User+Memory versus Core+PDLC+Memory:184 main + 12 restart assertions, independent audit and Astra acceptance. Final data retained; no database creation/deletion. [Verification and scope](https://github.com/arunmenon/Engram/blob/4bd47dd/docs/review/spanner-compatibility/tenant-isolation-verification.md).

This checkpoint does not close this issue. Tenant native webhooks/global metrics/import/cursors/prune/replay/reconsolidate, general pending/draining/forced termination and pilot readiness remain outside the accepted proof; hierarchy #49 remains parked. Earlier dated source observations below remain historical context, while the feature requirements remain open.

## Current agreed context — 2026-10-07

**Scope:** Confirmed target: one Spanner database per tenant, shared instance permitted; Engram routes authenticated context to that database and composed pack bundle.

**Required proof:** Define and implement minimal API/worker/search/retrieval/admin routing and scoped resource lifecycle, with colliding-ID isolation and no default-database fallback; a namespace or independent registry is not proof.

**Shared decisions:** Core is mandatory. Optional memory/user/domain capabilities compose through declared dependencies, without pairwise hardcoded flows. Authenticated tenant identity resolves its authorized Spanner database and pack bundle; processing and retrieval use that same context. Never infer authorization from agent_id, caller-chosen database or artifact IDs.

**Tracking and status:** Parent #34 holds the reconciled six-bucket scope; #35/#42 own composition/capability controls, #43 tenant routing, #39 exact conformance and #41 real-Spanner execution. This is a scope/context reconciliation, not a fresh runtime verification. The issue remains open; historical reproductions below retain their original revision, backend and run scope. Historical memory probes are diagnostic evidence, not cloud acceptance. No Redis/Neo4j runners or cross-backend migration are required. Pinned documentation links below are historical published snapshots; newer local reports/run artifacts remain unpublished unless explicitly linked to a published revision.

---

Parent: #34. Related: #35 activation/capabilities, #39 conformance, #41 Spanner verification. The database-per-tenant direction is confirmed. Define and implement the bounded tenant routing and activation needed by #34 using existing composition/storage patterns; no new multitenancy framework is presumed.

## Problem and evidence
Tenants may need different selected pack bundles (for example core+PDLC versus core+user+memory). Astra medium found one process-wide ontology registry at API startup; configured runtime caching keys configuration, not an authenticated tenant. API authentication checks shared keys without returning tenant context. Spanner ledger/graph/subscription keys and ontology active state have no established tenant dimension. Therefore different registry objects or different processes pointed at the same stores are not proof of tenant isolation.

Relevant source: src/context_graph/api/{app,dependencies}.py; ontology/{runtime,versioning}.py; adapters/spanner/{schema,subscription,log,graph}.py; ports/pack_graph.py; worker/extraction.py user identity construction.

## Confirmed direction and implementation boundary
Use one authorized Spanner database per tenant, with shared Spanner instance permitted. Authenticated tenant context selects the database and active composed pack bundle across API, workers and operations. A separate Engram deployment is not required by this decision; define minimal supported routing/client lifecycle and onboarding mapping before implementation. Separate configuration objects or caller-selected database names are not authorization.

## Acceptance
- [ ] Record the chosen deployment/tenant boundary, explicit supported customer scenarios and resource routing; distinguish today’s implementation from target behavior.
- [ ] Define ownership and scoping for ledger, graph/search, subscriptions/checkpoints, ontology/replay state, caches, APIs, admin/evaluation and retention. A caller-supplied header/agent_id alone is not a boundary.
- [ ] Define activation authorization, dependencies and interpretation-version agreement, plus disable/re-enable, historical visibility and catch-up policies with #35.
- [ ] Implement tenant-scoped ingress/handshake and required worker/read/admin routing from the reviewed boundary; split demonstrated missing work into bounded child tasks if necessary, preserving specialized processing.
- [ ] Specify adversarial tests using identical event/session/agent/artifact IDs across tenants, independent selected packs and admin/replay/cleanup operations. No cross-tenant reads, writes, acknowledgments or deletion.
- [ ] Verify database routing and complete API/worker/search/cache/admin separation even when the instance/application infrastructure is shared; prove failure isolation and no silent default database fallback.
- [ ] Add selected architecture’s acceptance to #39 and real-Spanner verification to #41; do not call local schema checks isolation proof.

Astra report and bounded schema probes are saved locally at docs/review/spanner-compatibility/2026-10-07-astra-pack-optionality-review.md and matching local-probe.py/.json; not yet published, no cloud tests performed.


## Required retrieval audit: only core may be assumed present

Confirmed product invariant: core is mandatory. Memory, user and every domain pack may be absent. Describing built-in schema in pack files does not mean all specialized retrieval code is already decoupled.

Current audit starting points include domain/pack_intents.py OPEN_PACKS partitioning, retrieval/engine.py intent/seed fallback, adapters/graph_ops.py user_profile and workflow_pattern seed branches, and retrieval/artifacts.py active domain seed/type/traversal selection. Specialized implementations may remain; availability must come from resolved selected capabilities rather than assumptions that all base packs are loaded.

- [ ] Inventory hardcoded type/edge/intent/seed/hydration/ranking/traversal/evidence and fallback dependencies in both event-memory and artifact retrieval paths, including storage/search adapter calls and any user endpoints.
- [ ] For core-only, core+PDLC, core+user, core+memory and combined selections, define supported queries and precise disabled/unsupported outcomes. No PDLC/user/memory presence may be assumed without active dependencies.
- [ ] Use the tenant's authenticated, server-resolved database and pack interpretation context for every retrieval call and cache, including search/vector results, graph expansion, evidence fetches and pagination cursors. Do not accept another tenant's supplied IDs/cursor as authorization or silently route to a default database.
- [ ] Test historical disabled-pack nodes and cross-pack edges: enforce explicit visibility policy rather than assuming seed filtering prevents traversal/evidence leakage. Define disable/re-enable/catch-up policy before executing affected tests.
- [ ] Verify unfamiliar compatible packs and unrelated-pack noninterference without combination-specific engine branches. A disabled required provider/capability must yield the defined error or refusal, not a misleading empty answer or hidden fallback.
- [ ] Bind concrete retrieval expectations to #39 fixtures and tracked #41 runs: exact typed artifact IDs, properties, relationships and supporting events; rejected/incomplete evidence behavior; colliding IDs across two tenant databases and negative isolation assertions.

This scope is required under #34. Local audit/checklists are not proof of implementation or real-Spanner acceptance.

items.title: Monthly Dashboard v2 — unified RAW/core/template for W + CPR
items.body:
## Goal

Build **Monthly Dashboard v2** as a shared architecture for W and CPR first, using the same raw data foundation as Daily/Weekly while preserving Monthly-specific business logic and visual structure.

Do **not** work on Orange yet. Do **not** spend time on visual polish or SKU-specific analysis until this task is complete.

## Core principles

1. **One raw data foundation**
   - Daily, Weekly and Monthly must read from the same normalized RAW layer in Supabase.
   - Monthly must not be derived from `sku_daily`.
   - Reports may apply different business logic, but must not maintain separate primary data sources.

2. **One Monthly template**
   - W and CPR must use one shared frontend/core implementation.
   - Cabinet-specific differences live in config/data, not duplicated code.
   - Architecture should be extensible to Orange and future clients after W/CPR are validated.

3. **Monthly lifecycle**
   - LIVE = current month.
   - CLOSING = previous month after cutoff, while validation/enrichment completes.
   - CLOSED = frozen month.
   - Month cutoff is 00:00 on the first day of the next month.
   - Closed month must not drift when order statuses change later.

4. **Compensations are separate**
   - Base Monthly economics must work without compensation/decompensation.
   - Compensation layer is applied independently later.
   - CPR logic: actual SKU compensation.
   - W/Orange logic later: category-level allocation.
   - For now, keep compensation excluded from the core validation of September.

## Existing verified September baseline

### W
- Finance API September 01–30 loaded to Supabase.
- Official Ozon accrual report reconciled exactly: **0.00 RUB difference**.
- Net sales: **6,387,302.00 RUB**
- Result after standard Ozon charges, before compensation: **2,034,525.91 RUB**
- September is now stored in `sku_monthly_w`.

### CPR
- Finance API September 01–30 loaded to Supabase.
- Official Ozon accrual report reconciled exactly: **0.00 RUB difference** at raw Finance level.
- Net sales: **7,159,659.00 RUB**
- Result before compensation/decompensation: **2,536,482.50 RUB**
- Difference to Ozon grand total = **8,533.90 RUB**, intentionally excluded decompensation.
- September is now stored in `sku_monthly_cpr`.

### Shared raw finance table
- `public.ozon_finance_lines_raw_v1`
- tenant_id distinguishes W / CPR.

## Required architecture

Target flow:

```
Ozon API
  -> shared RAW tables in Supabase
  -> normalized/core SQL layer
  -> Daily views
  -> Weekly views
  -> Monthly views
  -> shared Monthly frontend
```

n8n should be used for ingestion/schedules/integrations, not as the business-logic source of truth.

## Data layer tasks

### A. Audit current sources
Document what Daily, Weekly and Monthly currently read from for W and CPR.

Identify:
- duplicated sources;
- report-specific tables that are acting as primary data;
- hardcoded month/account logic;
- duplicated expense classification;
- any dependency on Google Sheets.

### B. Normalize raw entities
At minimum define/confirm shared raw sources for:
- orders/statuses;
- finance accrual lines;
- product/SKU dictionary;
- price history;
- cost history;
- business expenses;
- compensation imports.

Every shared source must include tenant/account identity.

### C. Central expense classification
Create one source of truth for Ozon fee classification:
- type_id;
- Ozon label;
- internal expense_group;
- direct/shared;
- allocation basis.

Daily/Weekly/Monthly must consume the same classification.

Unknown type_id must fail validation or appear in an explicit audit table; never silently go to an unreviewed bucket.

## Monthly core

Create a shared Monthly Core schema/view set parameterized by tenant.

Expected output per SKU/month should include at least:
- tenant_id / account_id;
- month;
- marketplace;
- SKU;
- article;
- product_name;
- master_category;
- sale_operations;
- return_operations;
- sold_units;
- sales;
- returns;
- net_sales;
- commission;
- logistics;
- storage;
- promotion;
- other;
- direct expenses;
- allocated shared expenses;
- total Ozon expenses;
- result without compensation;
- compensation placeholders;
- result with compensation;
- economic units;
- received per unit;
- source;
- month status: LIVE/CLOSING/CLOSED;
- updated_at.

Do not duplicate this logic for W and CPR.

## Month close mechanism

Implement a reusable closing process:

1. At 00:00 first day of next month, previous month leaves LIVE.
2. Freeze order/status snapshot.
3. Backfill full Finance API for all dates of previous month.
4. Validate completeness.
5. Store closed month result.
6. Current month becomes the only LIVE month.
7. Later data changes must not mutate CLOSED month membership.

If exact historical status at cutoff cannot be guaranteed from a current-state table, introduce append-only status history or another reliable capture mechanism.

## Validation / acceptance checks

Build automated checks for every closed month:

- every expected calendar day loaded;
- raw Finance total equals normalized Finance total;
- sum SKU + shared allocations equals account total;
- shared allocation conserves the original shared amount exactly;
- no unknown type_id;
- no duplicate accrual keys;
- no duplicated SKU/month rows;
- closed month is immutable;
- LIVE month remains dynamic;
- W September matches verified control:
  - net sales 6,387,302.00
  - result before compensation 2,034,525.91
- CPR September matches verified control:
  - net sales 7,159,659.00
  - result before compensation 2,536,482.50

Produce a validation report/query that can be run after every monthly close.

## Shared frontend

After the data/core layer is stable:

Create one Monthly frontend/template for W and CPR.

Cabinet differences must be configuration only.

Suggested structure:

```
monthly/
  core/
  config/
  data/
  components/
  tests/
```

No separate W Monthly app and CPR Monthly app.

### Monthly visual structure to preserve

Top KPI block:
1. Net sales
2. Marketplace expenses
3. Ozon result without compensation
4. Compensation
5. Business expenses
6. Final result after all expenses

Below:
- Financial funnel
- Month dynamics: 3 closed + current live
- Expense structure
- Business expenses/capital
- SKU table
- SKU detail card

The frontend must clearly label LIVE vs CLOSED.

## Dashboard data access

Current W/CPR management dashboards are served via n8n webhook and read SQL tables.

For v2:
- prefer a direct prepared API/view layer over using n8n as a read proxy;
- if keeping n8n temporarily, isolate it as transport only;
- frontend schema should be identical for every tenant.

Target API shape conceptually:
- `/monthly?tenant=W`
- `/monthly?tenant=CPR`

## Account config

Create a shared account configuration model/table with fields such as:
- tenant_id;
- marketplace;
- account_id;
- display_name;
- active;
- category/default master category;
- compensation method;
- cost method;
- business expense method;
- dashboard enabled.

Goal: onboarding another cabinet should be configuration-driven, not code duplication.

## Historical cost model

Costs must be time-valid:
- SKU
- valid_from
- valid_to
- unit_cost

Historical months must not change when a new cost is entered.

## Scope order

### Phase 1
Audit + unified RAW/data model.

### Phase 2
Shared Monthly Core for W + CPR.

### Phase 3
LIVE/CLOSING/CLOSED lifecycle + month close automation.

### Phase 4
Automated reconciliation/tests against July/August/September.

### Phase 5
Single Monthly frontend for W + CPR.

### Phase 6
Compensation layer.

### Phase 7
Business expenses + historical costs.

### Phase 8
Only after W/CPR are stable: Orange.

## Non-goals for this task

- No Orange migration yet.
- No SKU-specific pricing analysis.
- No cosmetic UI tweaks unless required for shared-template refactor.
- Do not change Daily business logic.
- Do not break Weekly.
- Do not delete legacy tables/views before parity is proven.

## Definition of done

Monthly v2 is complete when:

- W and CPR use one Monthly template.
- Daily/Weekly/Monthly share one RAW foundation.
- September is CLOSED without manual Excel dependence.
- October is the only LIVE month.
- Next month can transition automatically.
- Finance API reconciliation is automated.
- Expense classification is centralized.
- Unknown fees are surfaced.
- Historical costs are time-valid.
- New cabinets can be added by config.
- Legacy W/CPR monthly paths are archived only after parity tests pass.
- A short migration/readme document explains:
  - final architecture;
  - table/view ownership;
  - close workflow;
  - validation commands;
  - how to onboard a new cabinet.

## Delivery expectations

Work in small verifiable commits/PR(s). For each phase, include:
- what changed;
- impact on dashboard;
- how to verify it;
- any migration/backfill required.

Do not require the user to shuttle implementation details between ChatGPT and Codex. Keep implementation notes in the repository/issue/PR.
